Trump Makes Midterm Pitch to Farmers. An $8 billion aid package aims to take the edge off the strain of the Iran war and trade chaos.
Zelensky Seeks U.S. Support, but Is Trump Interested?. The White House appears increasingly focused on bolstering ties with Russia.
What Does Beijing Mean By ‘Strategic Stability’?. After the Trump summit, China wants managed competition.
Myanmar’s Shan State Is the World’s Meth Lab. Are illicit drugs now a bigger business in the Mekong than scam centers?
The Banking Scandal Upending Brazil’s Election. The country’s powerful Supreme Court is caught up in a swirling corruption probe.

Tehran hospital locks its main building and treats patients in the courtyard. A Social Security hospital in Tehran has locked its main building and moved treatment into a cramped clinic in its courtyard, a member of the insurer’s healthcare oversight committee said, two months after officials listed it among the capital’s unsafe hospitals.

German court jails two men over spying for Iran's Guards. A German court convicted two men of spying on prominent Jewish figures and preparing attacks against them on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force, sentencing both to prison on Thursday.

Armed suspect arrested over alleged plot to kill ex-minister, reformists say. An armed man was arrested over an alleged plot to assassinate a former Iranian minister after a gathering attended by Mohammad Khatami, the former president associated with efforts to reform the Islamic Republic from within, Iran’s Reform Front said.

Statement on a cyberattack targeting an Iran International correspondent. On 10 October 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to the work account of one of our correspondents. The correspondent was approached by someone posing as a representative of an established think tank and invited to join an online meeting.

Tehran hardline mayor rolls out economic relief: is he eyeing the presidency?. Tehran’s hardline mayor Alireza Zakani has drawn accusations of using municipal resources to prepare for another presidential bid after announcing a freeze on basic food prices and payments to new parents.

US alert puts Iran’s overseas religious finance networks under scrutiny. The US Treasury’s latest warning over Iran’s alleged abuse of religious charities puts renewed attention on religious and charitable organizations outside Iran that have separately faced criminal, regulatory or government scrutiny over financial or institutional links to Tehran.

Suspect in journalist attack plot says UK-based IRGC officer threatened to kill him. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists told a London court on Thursday that a man he identified as a Revolutionary Guards officer living in Britain threatened to kill him and his mother unless he obeyed.

Iran touts economic resilience while households struggle to afford basics. Iran’s central bank governor has dismissed claims of economic collapse, while domestic media reports describe wages failing to cover basic living costs and families struggling to afford medicines, housing and car repairs.

Iran speaker says government overstepped on anti-terror finance rules. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says part of the government’s anti-terror financing regulations violates Iranian law, adding that decisions on who is designated as terrorist must remain with the Supreme National Security Council.

Iran shipped jet fuel to Myanmar despite US blockade - Reuters. Iran managed to export jet fuel to Myanmar and send several shipments of liquefied petroleum gas out of the region despite a US naval blockade that has largely halted its crude exports, Reuters reported on Friday.

Norwegian teen gets 20-year sentence in UK murder plot linked to Iran. A Norwegian teenager recruited by a Swedish crime group linked by prosecutors to the Iranian government was sentenced to 20 years’ detention in Britain on Friday.

Iran’s rulers face a reckoning with their own people, former US envoy says. Decades of American sanctions strengthened Iran’s Revolutionary Guards by hollowing out the middle class, former US diplomat Joey Hood told Iran International, and once the fighting ends, Tehran will face a reckoning with its own people.

Iran hangs Iraqi man on Saudi spying charge he denied. Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.

Iranian court sentences woman to 50 lashes for kissing a man in a cafe. A court in the Iranian city of Qom has sentenced a woman to 50 lashes for kissing and hugging a man in a cafe, after her husband filed a complaint and submitted video of the meeting, according to the rights group HRANA. She denies the charge.

Iran raided, summoned and jailed Baha’is in Yazd 34 times in seven months. Iranian security and judicial authorities have taken action against Baha’is in the central city of Yazd at least 34 times in less than seven months, raiding homes, summoning dozens for interrogation and jailing members of the faith, the rights group HRANA reported on Friday.

After the killings, Iran turned on the families of the dead. A bullet is fired once. For the families of those killed in Iran’s Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, the punishment that followed lasted for years: bodies held hostage, false confessions forced on parents, funerals fired upon and killers set free, Amnesty International has found.

Iran cultivated Houthis for years before opening new war front, insider says. Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.

Iran giving Houthis targeting intelligence for Saudi attacks - WSJ. Iranian support has helped Yemen’s Houthis carry out their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on intelligence from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s anti-Houthi alliance.

Iran's January crackdown: Snipers at Friday prayer leader's office, dorm. Iran's security forces deployed snipers on the rooftops of the provincial Friday prayer leader's office and a women's student dormitory to fire on protesters during January's deadly crackdown in Semnan, east of Tehran, an Iran International investigation found.

Tehran’s diplomatic paralysis leaves Iran caught between deal and escalation. A growing number of former Iranian officials and political figures are calling for an agreement with the United States, while hardliners and military commanders continue to push for confrontation, exposing a deeper struggle over the direction of Tehran’s foreign policy.

Iran risks losing ground as East-West trade routes expand. Investment in trade routes linking Asia and Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus is putting pressure on Iran’s ambitions to become a major transit hub, with neighboring countries developing transport and digital networks that bypass Iranian territory.

Who are the Baluch militants taking on Iran rulers, and how far can they go?. A wave of deadly attacks on Iranian security forces in the country’s restive southeast has brought renewed attention to a coalition of Baluch militants seeking to broaden their fight against the Islamic Republic, raising questions about how far the insurgency can spread.

Architect of Guards' missiles becomes Iran's defense minister. Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, a sanctioned veteran of Iran's missile industry with ties to the Revolutionary Guards, became defense minister on Sunday, following his predecessor's killing in the war with the United States and Israel.

Iran signals possible nuclear policy shift, threatens US retaliation. Iranian officials raised the possibility of a shift in nuclear policy and threatened retaliation against further US-Israeli attacks, while Tehran outlined its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.

Trump says US may ‘soon finish the job’ on Iran, Netanyahu vows to topple regime. US President Donald Trump on Sunday warned Washington could “soon finish the job” against Iran unless Tehran changed course, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was prepared to strike Iran without US support and vowed to bring down Tehran’s government.

Iran rolls out regional Data Authority amid threats to Mideast tech infrastructure. Iran's parliament speaker said a "Persian Gulf Data Authority" was coming and urged regional governments and investors to withhold resources from AI companies involved in military operations, amid Tehran threats against digital infrastructure across the region.

Retirees protest across Iran over economic hardship, repression. Retirees staged protests in several Iranian cities on Sunday over soaring living costs, inadequate pensions and healthcare problems, with some demonstrators also chanting against government corruption, repression and executions.

US and Israel threaten renewed Iran strikes, Tehran warns of response. US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu escalated threats against Iran on Sunday, and Tehran warned of retaliation even as diplomatic efforts continued over the Strait of Hormuz and the wider conflict.

Soaring medical costs and staff shortages strain Iran’s hospitals. People in Iran have described deteriorating hospital services, rising treatment costs, shortages of medical staff and equipment, and long waits for care, as healthcare workers struggle with low wages and growing workloads, according to accounts shared with Iran International.

Iranians report mass security warnings over social media activity. Iran's police intelligence agency has sent threatening text messages warning citizens of possible prosecution over online activity, including people who do not use social media, according to accounts shared with Iran International.

Teenager killed by gunshot to eye after arrest in Iran, source says. An 18-year-old mechanic was killed by a gunshot to his right eye after being wounded and detained on January 9, according to information obtained by Iran International from a source close to his family.

Iran threatens stronger response to new US attack as Lavrov visits Tehran. Iranian military officials warned of a stronger response to any renewed US attack on Monday, as Russia's foreign minister visited Tehran for talks and regional security concerns grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Iranians react to French protests with ‘karma’ and memories of 1979 revolution. Ongoing protests and unrest in France prompted Iranian commenters to revisit the country’s role in the 1979 Islamic Revolution and criticize Western responses to crackdowns in Iran, with many calling the turmoil “karma” in response to an Iran International Instagram question.

Ex-president's remarks expose divide over costs of Iran’s Palestine policy. Former President Mohammad Khatami’s criticism of the costs of Iran’s intervention in Palestinian affairs has fueled debate over Tehran’s policy, with hardliners defending its role and some opponents of the Islamic Republic questioning the motives behind his remarks.

Over a dozen Iranian women and girls killed in 30 days, many by male relatives. At least 15 women and girls have been reported killed across Iran over the past month, many allegedly by husbands, brothers or other male relatives, Iranian news outlet Rokna reported, as legislation aimed at protecting women from violence remains stalled.

Russia vows continued Iran ties as Trump welcomes limits on support. Russia pledged to maintain its political and economic cooperation with Iran during Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's visit to Tehran on Monday, as US President Donald Trump welcomed what he described as limited Russian and Chinese support for Tehran.

Iran deal remains elusive amid risk of renewed strikes. Washington and Tehran may still reach a limited deal, but fundamental disagreements leave open the prospect of renewed escalation, analysts told Iran International, with the period after elections in Israel and the United States emerging as a potential turning point.

Iran’s threats ring out from parliament struggling to meet or connect. Iran’s new defense minister threatened the US and Israel during a parliamentary session held online over fears of attack, but even the virtual meeting faltered when poor internet connections prevented 25 lawmakers from voting on his appointment.

Iran Air chief says 30 to 40 operational aircraft destroyed in war. Between 30 and 40 of Iran’s operational aircraft were destroyed during the war, while another 70 to 80 were hit, Iran Air chief executive Taher Abdolhai said on Monday.

Saudi Arabia should join US-led push for change in Iran, analyst says. Saudi Arabia should join forces with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates to help bring about political change in Iran, rather than continue policies that have failed to contain Tehran's regional influence, an analyst told Iran International.

Iran-Pakistan border trade halt leaves trucks and cargo stranded. Trade between Iran and Pakistan remained suspended at two major border crossings on Tuesday, leaving trucks and cargo stranded, with Pakistani authorities citing security and anti-smuggling measures and Iran pointing to technical difficulties.

Toppling Iran’s regime is ‘primary objective,’ Netanyahu says after US talks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that toppling Iran’s regime was Israel’s “primary objective,” a day after discussing Iran with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth during an unannounced visit to Israel.

Pakistani mediator leaves Tehran after Iran doubles down on demands. Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir left Tehran on Tuesday after Iranian leaders reiterated their conditions for negotiations with Washington and ruled out transferring enriched nuclear material abroad, as regional mediators continue efforts to ease the standoff.

Iran in Israeli election: Netanyahu all-in on regime change, rivals want more. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making regime change in Iran an explicit goal ahead of Israel’s election, while political rivals advocate tough measures against Tehran and criticize his failure to eliminate the Iranian threat.

Iran hardliners split over role of mediators in US tensions. Renewed efforts to avert another war with the United States drew conflicting responses in Tehran, with hardliners questioning mediators’ motives while officials defended keeping diplomatic channels open.

Iran accused of stoking French unrest through influence operations. Iran is seeking to amplify unrest in France through online influence campaigns and alleged links to hard-left groups, The Times reported on Tuesday, citing researchers who accused Tehran and Moscow of exploiting student protests to weaken Western democracies.

Ghalibaf allies seek an end to war without giving up leverage over US. A current within Iran’s conservative establishment associated with Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf favors maintaining military and economic leverage while keeping open the possibility of a negotiated end to the war with the United States.

Iranian women killed by relatives after seeking divorce or refusing marriage. Asking for a divorce, refusing a marriage, speaking to a man she did not know: in Iran, each has preceded the killing of a woman or girl by her own family, according to a Shargh daily investigation that counted at least 38 dead in two months.

Iranian applicants protest German visa delays in Tehran. Iranians seeking German work and vocational-training visas protested outside the German Embassy in Tehran on Tuesday over lengthy delays in securing appointments, with some saying they had already lost job offers or training places while waiting.

IRGC threatens undersea cables, but can it disrupt global internet?. The Revolutionary Guards' threat to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz raises questions about its feasibility, as the waterway carries a fraction of global bandwidth and damaging its cables would not shut down the world's internet.

En Ouganda, comment Muhoozi Kainerugaba étend son influence de l’armée à la politique. Depuis la réélection de Yoweri Museveni en janvier 2026, l’emprise du chef d’état-major de l’armée sur son pays ne cesse de croître. Du Parlement au gouvernement en passant par la sphère économique, il a continué à étendre son réseau, se positionnant plus que jamais comme le successeur de son père.

Cameroun : sur la route Douala-Yaoundé, sept heures pour parcourir 230 kilomètres. Le délabrement de la route Douala-Yaoundé exaspère les usagers et inquiète jusqu’aux cadres du parti au pouvoir. Alors que le gouvernement annonce de nouveaux travaux, le financement et les délais de reconstruction restent des défis majeurs.

Touadéra et les rebelles : en Centrafrique, l’interminable bras de fer entre le président et les groupes armés. Le gouvernement centrafricain s’active pour signer, en novembre à Bangui, un nouvel accord consacrant la réhabilitation de certains chefs rebelles, parmi lesquels Mahamat al-Khatim, Ali Darassa et Sembé Bobo. Mais l’est du pays reste menacé par un ancien allié de ces derniers, Noureddine Adam.

Au Mali, les compagnies minières prises entre étau fiscal et casse-tête logistique. Confrontées à la hausse des redevances, à la dégradation des conditions sécuritaires ou encore à des différends juridiques avec la junte au pouvoir, les sociétés minières naviguent dans un environnement de plus en plus incertain.

RDC : la discrète médiation finlandaise entre l’opposition et le pouvoir. Des représentants de la majorité et de l’opposition ont été invités en septembre pour un séjour de trois jours à Helsinki. Objectif : favoriser le dialogue avec un cadre plus informel et détendu.

AES-Cedeao : les deux blocs annoncent vouloir travailler à un « accord-cadre ». Dans un communiqué conjoint samedi soir, les deux parties se « sont félicitées de l’esprit de fraternité » des discussions et ont affiché l’ambition de parvenir à un accord-cadre de coopération.

Érythrée-Éthiopie : entre Issayas Afewerki et Abiy Ahmed, le retour de la guerre. La reprise de la guerre dans le Tigré fait planer la menace d’un conflit ouvert entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée. Issayas Afewerki et Abiy Ahmed, un temps alliés, se livrent une bataille des ambitions sur fond de retournements d’alliances inédits.

Joseph Kabila, « proxy » de Paul Kagame ?. En prenant les rênes du mouvement rebelle FRN, Joseph Kabila bouscule l’échiquier politique et militaire congolais. Décryptage d’une alliance opportuniste avec le Rwanda.

Cameroun : Tiriane Noah à la tête du MRC, entre fidélité à Maurice Kamto et défis internes. L’opposante a été élue à la tête du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun, principal parti d’opposition camerounais. Elle succède à Maurice Kamto, déjà annoncé comme le candidat du parti à la prochaine présidentielle.

Au Maroc, combien coûtera le stade Hassan-II ?. Appelé à devenir le plus grand du monde avec 115 000 places, le stade doit être achevé d’ici la fin de 2027. Alors que son budget initial a déjà été multiplié par 2,7, la question de sa rentabilisation se pose déjà.

Côte d’Ivoire – Ahoua Don Mello : « Qui peut vaincre la Russie de Vladimir Poutine ? Personne ». Ses relations avec le chef de l’État russe, Africa Corps, la guerre en Ukraine… L’ancien ministre de Laurent Gbagbo détaille son partenariat avec Moscou et évoque également la création de son parti, La Côte d’Ivoire souveraine, ainsi que ses désaccords avec l’opposition. Entretien.

Massacre de Shakaloha au Kenya : Paul Mackenzie jugé coupable du meurtre de 191 personnes. Déjà poursuivi par la justice pour le meurtre d’environ 450 fidèles qu’il aurait poussés au suicide, le gourou autoproclamé a été reconnu coupable d’homicide sur 190 enfants et un adulte.

Minerais critiques : pourquoi les banques de développement font leur grand retour dans le secteur. L’accélération de la demande mondiale et la rivalité autour des approvisionnements poussent les grandes institutions financières internationales à revoir leur positionnement dans le secteur minier.

Cameroun : dans les coulisses de la guerre entre Eko Eko et Ngoh Ngoh. Le procès Martinez Zogo met en lumière les rivalités au sommet de l’appareil sécuritaire camerounais. L’ancien patron du renseignement accuse le secrétaire général de la présidence d’avoir manœuvré contre lui. Deux rapports confidentiels consultés par Jeune Afrique éclairent les ressorts de leur affrontement.

Au Maroc, la sortie en clair-obscur d’Aziz Akhannouch. Le prochain chapitre du parcours du chef de gouvernement sortant se dessine déjà loin de la politique. Entre confidences de son entourage, retour annoncé aux affaires et ambitions de ceux qui lorgnent son héritage politique, les coulisses d’un retrait.

Comment la loterie nationale de Côte d’Ivoire résiste à la concurrence en ligne. Malgré la percée fulgurante d’acteurs privés du pari en ligne, la Lonaci affiche des résultats records. Grâce à son statut de régulateur, la loterie nationale profite de la dynamique de ses concurrents privés.

Appel à la grève générale au Sénégal à la veille des premiers JOJ en Afrique. Face au risque de grève générale à Dakar, le gouvernement sénégalais multiplie les appels au dialogue avec le FSDT. L’exécutif cherche à éviter toute perturbation avant le coup d’envoi historique des Jeux olympiques de la Jeunesse.

Le Burkina interdit la privatisation des entreprises publiques à « caractère stratégique ». Les députés burkinabè ont adopté une loi barrant la privatisation des entreprises publiques d’intérêt national. Cette mesure concrétise la ligne souverainiste d’Ibrahim Traoré, du secteur de la défense à celui des infrastructures.

L’opposant rwandais en exil Robert Kabera retrouvé mort en Ouganda. L’ancien sergent rwandais a été retrouvé décapité près de Kampala. Cet assassinat relance les soupçons sur la traque des opposants à Paul Kagame au-delà des frontières du Rwanda.

Côte d’Ivoire : 5 questions pour comprendre comment la pression judiciaire s’accroît sur Tidjane Thiam. Alors que la justice ivoirienne doit examiner le 22 octobre les requêtes formulées par des membres de son parti, le PDCI, qui visent à annuler son élection, l’opposant en exil voit également plusieurs de ses cadres convoqués par la justice.

Mines, télécoms, usines… Les industriels africains réussiront-ils à se passer du diesel ?. Le diesel reste indispensable au fonctionnement de nombreuses activités sur le continent. Mais son coût, les contraintes d’approvisionnement et les impératifs de décarbonation poussent les industriels à accélérer le recours aux solutions renouvelables.

Massacre au Mali : l’État islamique s’attaque à la communauté idaksahak dans la région de Ménaka. L’attaque terroriste de l’État islamique a coûté la vie à au moins 48 civils dans la région de Ménaka, au Mali. Ce massacre, visant la communauté idaksahak et perpétré en représailles aux opérations militaires, marque une tragique escalade.

En Guinée-Bissau, la junte cherche-t-elle à évincer Embaló ?. Hier soupçonné par l’opposition d’être de mèche avec les putschistes qui l’avaient pourtant renversé, l’ex-président Umaro Sissoco Embaló se retrouve aujourd’hui empêché de regagner Bissau, sur fond de purge parmi ses proches et de report sine die de la présidentielle.

Abidjan-Paris : le tandem Air France-Air Côte d’Ivoire resserre l’étau autour de Corsair. En mutualisant la commercialisation de leurs vols entre Paris et Abidjan, Air France et Air Côte d’Ivoire renforcent leur offre sans ajouter de fréquences. Cette alliance commerciale accentue la pression sur Corsair, seul concurrent direct des deux partenaires sur cette ligne.

Cameroun : comment le schisme entre Nourane Foster et Cabral Libii fragilise le PCRN à Douala. Élue en 2020 sous les couleurs du PCRN de Cabral Libii, Nourane Foster en a claqué la porte fin septembre, entraînant une partie des militants de Douala. À quelques mois des législatives, elle menace désormais son ancien parti dans son fief.

Face à Ethiopian Airlines, le périlleux redressement de Kenya Airways et South African Airways. Dans l’ombre d’Ethiopian Airlines, les deux entreprises suivent des voies contrastées et fragiles vers la viabilité financière, tout en s’efforçant d’attirer des investisseurs stratégiques.

« Le sentimentalisme, c’est fini » : au Burkina Faso, Ibrahim Traoré rétablit la peine de mort. Huit ans après son abolition, la peine de mort a été réintroduite ce mardi dans le code pénal burkinabè. Un virage sécuritaire assumé par la junte au pouvoir, qui y voit un moyen de lutter contre le terrorisme et l’espionnage.

Au Maroc, le gouvernement El Mansouri marque déjà sa différence avec l’ère Akhannouch. À première vue, le programme de Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri s’inscrit dans le prolongement des grands chantiers engagés par Aziz Akhannouch. Mais une lecture croisée des deux déclarations gouvernementales révèle de vrais changements de cap, certains plaçant la nouvelle majorité face à ses propres contradictions.

Avec Somagec, Roger Sahyoun s’impose comme le visage atypique du BTP marocain. Sous la direction de l’ingénieur de 74 ans, Somagec est devenu un géant marocain diversifié dont les activités s’étendent de l’Afrique subsaharienne à l’Amérique du Sud. Pour se développer, il compte sur le marché financier et non sur les banques.

Paul Barril, le « barbouze » français au cœur du génocide des Tutsi au Rwanda. L’ancien du Groupement d’intervention de la gendarmerie nationale français est décédé ce 20 octobre. Reconverti dans le privé en Afrique, il était surtout tristement célèbre sur le continent pour son implication au côté du régime génocidaire rwandais.

Au Burkina Faso, le président Ibrahim Traoré crée une « ligue de la souveraineté » de football après une lourde défaite de l’équipe nationale. Le chef de la junte au pouvoir n’a pas digéré la déroute de la sélection nationale (0-7) face à l’Argentine et veut étendre sa « révolution » au ballon rond.

Au Maroc, un nouveau gouvernement formé, mais peu de changement, sauf pour les femmes. Trente-deux ministres ont prêté serment devant le roi du pays, Mohammed VI, vendredi 16 octobre, mais 40 % d’entre eux étaient déjà en poste. Les femmes, elles, reculent dans la hiérarchie gouvernementale.

Entre la RDC et la Belgique, des tensions après des perquisitions menées dans la famille du président congolais. La première dame et huit autres proches de Félix Tshisekedi sont au cœur d’une instruction pour blanchiment d’argent, ouverte par la justice belge en 2025. Après des perquisitions menées dans le plat pays, mercredi 14 octobre, le chef de l’Etat congolais a interdit à son gouvernement « tout contact » avec l’ambassade de Belgique.

« Dès qu’une tête dépasse, il la coupe » : Muhoozi Kainerugaba, héritier brutal et fantasque du président ougandais. Le fils du chef de l’Etat, déjà à la tête des forces armées et successeur présumé de son père à la présidence, est accusé de multiples violations des droits humains et enchaîne, sur les réseaux sociaux, les tirades aussi baroques que terrifiantes.

A Madagascar, un an après avoir été renversé, l’ex-président Andry Rajoelina rêve encore d’un retour sur la Grande Ile. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (3/4). Vivant en exil depuis octobre 2025, l’ancien chef de l’Etat s’efforce de mobiliser son réseau diplomatique loin de son pays, même si ses leviers d’action demeurent limités.

En Tunisie, plusieurs milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi dans les rues de la capitale, malgré la répression du régime de Kaïs Saïed. Depuis le coup de force du président tunisien, il y a cinq ans, une chape de plomb s’est abattue sur le pays. Une marche s’est malgré tout tenue à Tunis samedi 17 octobre, à l’appel de nombreuses organisations syndicales et de la société civile.

Comment l’administration de Donald Trump utilise des pays africains pour expulser des migrants en dépit du droit international. Sur les 28 000 immigrés expulsés des Etats-Unis entre le début de 2025 et août 2026, plus de 500 ont été envoyés sur le continent africain, selon les données du Deportation Data Project. La plupart du temps, ils n’ont pas de lien direct avec les pays d’Afrique.

Au Mali, plus de 40 civils tués par des hommes armés dans la région de Ménaka, selon des sources locales. Ces attaques sanglantes ont visé des campements appartenant majoritairement à la communauté des Daoussahak, dont est issu le groupe armé Mouvement pour le salut de l’Azawad, proche de la junte au pouvoir à Bamako, d’après des sources interrogées par l’Agence France-Presse.

En Algérie, les commentaires non autorisés sur l’économie exposent à des sanctions. La condamnation à quatre ans de prison d’un universitaire pour ses propos sur l’industrie extractive fait suite à la rétrogradation d’un ministre en vue en raison de ses propos dénonçant l’envolée des prix de la tomate.

Soudan : 53 morts après une attaque de l’armée soudanaise contre un marché à la frontière avec le Soudan du Sud. Le bilan pourrait « malheureusement s’alourdir », ont prévenu les autorités locales. Dimanche et lundi, plusieurs frappes au Soudan avaient fait près de 100 morts dans des zones aux mains des paramilitaires des Forces de soutien rapide.

Se laisser mourir de faim pour « rencontrer Jésus » : au Kenya, le gourou Paul Mackenzie reconnu coupable du meurtre de 190 enfants. Après treize mois d’audience, et l’audition de plus de 120 témoins, le premier procès du pasteur autoproclamé, accusé de l’une des pires tragédies de l’histoire du pays, s’est achevé lundi 19 octobre. Le prononcé de la peine aura lieu ultérieurement.

Madagascar, nouvelle terre de recrutement et d’influence pour la Russie. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (4/4). Mi-août, la mort sur le front ukrainien d’un Malgache enrôlé par l’armée russe a mis en lumière la discrète campagne de recrutement militaire sur la Grande Ile. Depuis l’arrivée du colonel Randrianirina, le pays a entamé un rapprochement généralisé avec la Russie, au grand dam de Paris.

Au Kenya, un gourou est reconnu coupable du meurtre de 190 enfants. Le pasteur autoproclamé Paul Nthenge Mackenzie prônait de jeûner jusqu’à la mort pour « rencontrer Jésus ». Il est reconnu coupable de la mort de 191 fidèles.

En Egypte, le président assure qu’il quittera le pouvoir en 2030, mais œuvre à la pérennité de son régime militaire. Dans deux discours prononcés la semaine du 12 octobre, Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi, au pouvoir depuis 2013, a annoncé qu’il ne briguerait pas de quatrième mandat. D’ici à 2030, il veillera toutefois à ce que ses éventuels successeurs soient sélectionnés et formés par la hiérarchie militaire.

La ratification par la Libye d’un accord maritime avec la Turquie redessine les lignes régionales. Le vote par le Parlement, basé à Benghazi, d’un accord turco-libyen de délimitation des zones économiques exclusives promet de causer des frictions avec l’Egypte et la Grèce, hostiles à cet arrangement.

'There is no life left': How volunteers buried 600 bodies in Sudan's North Kordofan Submitted by Mohammed Amin on Wed, 10/21/2026 - 07:30 Graphic warning: videos, photos and testimony obtained by MEE reveal devastation left by massacres as Sudan's war continues A volunteer buries a body in Bara, North Kordofan, Sudan (MEE) Off It took 50 volunteers to collect and bury more than 600 corpses. The streets of Bara, in Sudan ’s North Kordofan state, were lined with dead bodies. They were scattered in the surrounding villages. They were left on the road that links Bara to the state capital, the strategically vital city of el-Obeid. Most of them were killed, eyewitnesses said, in revenge attacks carried out by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) . The pile-up of large numbers of dead bodies has turned Bara into a depopulated wasteland, its ground poisoned and beset by insects and scorpions. Unknown disease is spreading rapidly because of the corpses, with the volunteers, who wear protective suits and masks, working as hard as they can to dispose safely of the remains. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Videos and photos shared exclusively with Middle East Eye show the victims of massacres that took place during a period of intense fighting in July, when the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) took the area back from the RSF. Multiple local sources, including activists and volunteers who participated in the process of retrieving and burying the dead, told MEE that most of the bodies were civilians. The rest were fighters, from both the SAF and RSF. The body of a Sudanese person killed in Bara, North Kordofan (MEE) On top of the more than 600 bodies that have been collected, the sources say there are hundreds more still left rotting in Bara and the surrounding countryside. The activists, including the independent Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), as well as volunteers from the popular resistance who have operated under the SAF’s command, accused the paramilitary RSF, which is sponsored by the United Arab Emirates and has been found by the UN and US to have committed genocide , of carrying out massacres and mass killings in the Bara area in October 2025. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mass graves and exposed corpses One volunteer told MEE that they had opened 200 mass graves in the area and then given a proper burial to all the corpses piled up inside. The source said that 400 other bodies had been buried. “These efforts have been financed by many local groups including the women and men of Bara, as well as others in the diaspora, particularly those living in Gulf countries, and others in el-Obeid,” he explained. The Sudanese health ministry, Sudanese Red Crescent and other local initiatives provided the volunteers with cases and bags, the source said. The group is still engaged in a process of cleaning and sanitisation in order not to spread disease. “We still need a lot of logistics and supplies including fuel, gloves, face masks, sanitisers, cases and bags, among other materials,” the volunteer said. “These corpses were found in the streets and squares as well as inside the houses,” Abdul Rahman, a leading member of the Bara resistance committee, told MEE. “Others have been found in villages around Bara and the process is still ongoing as we believe that the number is higher than what we have from field reports.” A volunteer placing a body into a bag (MEE) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Abdul Rahman said there were hundreds of bodies still stranded in areas around Bara, including in Geraigikh, Jabrat al-Sheikh and Umm Syala. The Sudanese information ministry has claimed that RSF violations have extended to more than 100 villages around Bara, with the area’s entire population having to flee their homes because of the attacks. After a recent meeting between Bara’s local leaders and the Sudanese Information Minister Khalid Ismail Ahmed Ali el-Aisir, the ministry said the government would support victims of RSF violations by helping with medical care and reconstruction. Bodies turned to skeletons The photos and videos shared exclusively with MEE and published here show dead bodies that lay out in the open for months. Some of the bodies had decomposed, while others had already turned into skeletons, a process that can take just a few weeks in a hot climate like Sudan’s. Dozens of volunteers wearing gloves and protected uniforms collected the bodies, some of which had become simply a collection of bones. They packed them into old cars or pick-up trucks and buried them collectively. The skeletons were of all different ages, including children and elderly people. Other, fresher bodies were of military personnel. Volunteers described brutal conditions, dirty and poisoned ground beset by swarms of butterflies and other insects, visited by scorpions and littered with dead animals and birds. Bodies decompose quickly as they are left out for months (MEE) "There is now no life left in Bara," one volunteer told MEE. The environment has totally collapsed because the vast number of dead bodies has resulted in the rapid spread of unknown diseases, they said. “This work is hard, and we do it without direct help from the authorities or the international NGOs. The only thing we got are the mortuary bags from the Sudanese Red Crescent,” the volunteer said. “The majority of the corpses we have retrieved from Bara and other villages are civilians killed in revenge attacks in the city after the RSF entered it last year,” Ismail Karam Aldin, a volunteer and popular resistance member, told MEE over the phone. “These efforts are only done by the volunteers of Bara’s people led by the popular resistance in the city. The Red Crescent and the local ministry of health have only provided the cases and bags to keep the corpses and bury them.” Sudan war continues along with external involvement Sudan’s war began in April 2023 and is now the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, with over 11 million people forcibly displaced from their homes and at least 150,000 believed to be dead. Both the SAF and RSF have been accused of committing war crimes, while the RSF has been found to have carried out genocide in different parts of Darfur, western Sudan. The RSF is supported by the UAE, though Abu Dhabi continues to deny its involvement despite mounting evidence, including from the UN fact-finding mission for Sudan. A group of volunteers pictured in Bara, Sudan (MEE) On Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke in front of a map that divided Sudan between the RSF-held west, which was listed as being friendly to Israel and the UAE, and the rest of the country, which was listed as being friendly to Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan. The SAF is supported militarily by Turkey and Egypt ; the latter recently killed at least 114 people in an air strike on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border. In Sudan’s deserted Bara, blood waters its famous lemon trees Read More » North Kordofan has seen a wide SAF military advance in recent weeks, with the army taking control of Sodar, Um Badir, al-Mazroub and other areas, leaving most of the state back in its control. A military source told MEE that the SAF would advance towards neighbouring West Kordofan state, particularly the cities of Al-Nuhud and Al-Khuwayyi, which are in regions rich in gum arabic. Previously, these areas produced more than 80 percent of the world’s gum arabic, an ingredient that is vital for multinational companies like Coca Cola and Pepsi and is also used in medicines in cosmetics. For its part, the RSF has widened drone attacks on the entire country, including on el-Obeid, Kosti in White Nile state, Atbara in the north, the capital Khartoum and its twin city Omdurman. Israel's vision of regional security rests on keeping Arab states weak Submitted by Mohamad Elmasry on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:44 Six years after the Abraham Accords, a new report by a former Israeli intelligence chief outlines a doctrine treating peace deals as temporary and regional instability as an asset Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif al-Zayani, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, US President Donald Trump and UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed after signing the Abraham Accords at the White House on 15 September 2020 (Saul Loeb/AFP) Off The 2020 Abraham Accords did not bring a new era of regional peace, as US President Donald Trump promised. Instead, since the agreements were signed, Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza and an unprecedented settlement expansion in the West Bank. No one, least of all experts, is surprised. From the moment the United Arab Emirates , Bahrain and Morocco formally normalised relations with Israel in 2020, the agreements - named the Abraham Accords by US President Donald Trump - were widely dismissed by critics as a farce. Even before the accords were signed, Middle East experts argued that they represented an act of political theatre and deception, seemingly throwing the Palestinian cause under the bus while pretending to create peace and brotherhood between the " sons of Abraham ". Shortly before the signings, British-Palestinian academic Kamel Hawwash said the Israelis were taking the Emiratis "for a ride" that promised the continuation and acceleration of Israel's occupation and apartheid policies. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Around the same time, Joseph Massad, a professor of modern Arab politics, described the accords as a way of rewriting "the horrific colonial reality of Zionism and Israel in terms of religious and fraternal discord". A new Israeli security report may provide important insights into Israel's strategic thinking when it signed the accords, as well as its policies in the years since. Even before the accords were signed, Middle East experts argued that they represented an act of political theatre and deception In the report, published on 12 October by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), Tamir Hayman, a former head of Israeli military intelligence who now runs the institute, sets out what he calls Israel's "new security policy". The report states that Israel does not view Arab countries as true nations, but instead as mere " collections of tribes and ethnic groups". As a result, undermining their stability "is viewed as a natural process" that Israel "should even encourage". Indeed, the policy treats weak, fragmented Arab states as a source of security, since instability is something Israel "can manage more effectively than it can contend with strong nation-states". It further defines Israel's approach as "perpetual preemptive war", with Israeli expansion - including into Syria and Lebanon - serving a broad objective of Arab "destabilization". Destabilisation in practice Hayman argues that Israel considers Middle East peace agreements as fundamentally "unattainable". When agreements are signed, they are "merely technical and temporary arrangements" designed to serve Israeli strategic objectives. This is key to understanding not only how Israel approaches the Abraham Accords, but also its current regional posture, from Gaza and the West Bank to Syria and Lebanon. Almost as soon as Syrians overthrew the longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Israel started working to destabilise the country. Israel's 'pilot zones' turn Lebanese sovereignty on its head Belen Fernandez Read More » The Israeli military has reportedly carried out hundreds of attacks on Syrian territory, destroyed much of Syria's defence capabilities, occupied large swaths of territory and armed militia groups opposed to the new government. In Lebanon, Israel has been arguably even more aggressive. There, it occupies between six percent and 20 percent of Lebanese territory. Since signing a ceasefire agreement with Hezbollah in November 2024, Israel has repeatedly attacked Lebanon, killing thousands . For the past several months, Israel has been engaged in peace talks with the Lebanese government. American mediators said in June that a tentative framework signed by Israeli and Lebanese leaders would lead to a "comprehensive peace" between the two countries. The security doctrine outlined by Hayman, however, suggests that Israel may have signed the agreement as cover for continuing its occupation and further destabilising Lebanon. Indications are that Israel has no intention of withdrawing from the Lebanese territory it has occupied. Hayman admits his report is partly subjective and that Israeli leadership has not formally acknowledged the new security doctrine he outlines. Recent Israeli conduct, however, makes Hayman's analysis certainly plausible, if not probable. His background as former head of military intelligence adds weight to his interpretation. A widening war If Hayman's basic premises are accurate, the implications for the Middle East could be deeply troubling. Israel may continue pursuing territorial expansion and Palestinian displacement in Gaza and the West Bank, while consolidating positions in Syria and Lebanon. Its confrontation with Iran could also escalate, with devastating consequences for the region. The US-Israeli war on Iran has already generated significant chaos, including ongoing spillover into Yemen and Saudi Arabia . Israel would welcome the Saudi-led war against Yemen's Houthis spreading further into the region, particularly if the widening conflict leads to additional destabilisation in important Arab countries. In this context, Egypt 's possible entry into the Yemen war on Saudi Arabia's side could serve Israeli strategic interests. On 17 October, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested parliamentary approval to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh asks for it. Parliament has since postponed its vote until 26 October. If Egypt does join the war, Israel could benefit in one of two ways. On the one hand, the swift crushing of the Houthis would eliminate a threat to Israel and allow Israeli leaders to boast of the defeat as a successful extension of their 28 February attack on Iran. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); On the other hand, if Egyptian help does not finish off the Houthis, the war could further widen. If nothing else, prolonged Egyptian involvement could drain resources and bog down a large, important Arab country on Israel's doorstep. Furthermore, Israel's strategic partnership with the UAE deserves scrutiny. As I have previously argued , the two countries share interests in weakening and fragmenting Arab states. Both countries have supported non-state separatist actors across the region. Normalisation as cover Even the two countries that normalised relations with Israel decades ago - Egypt and Jordan - have reason to be concerned. Since the start of the Gaza genocide, Israel has been accused of violating its Camp David agreement with Egypt. During the genocide, Israel took control of the Philadelphi Corridor, and more recently it has built new military fortifications in Rafah, a few kilometres from the Egyptian border. Earlier this month, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich issued an explicit threat to Egypt, warning that there would be "no Sinai" if it attacked Israel. Arab governments seeking security through normalisation may instead be helping to undermine their own Last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu expressed support for " Greater Israel ", raising concerns in Jordan that Israel planned to expand beyond the Palestinian territories. Despite all this, Arab governments continue to cooperate with Israel. Morocco upgraded its diplomatic relations with Israel last month, and Netanyahu travelled to the UAE in late September for talks that reportedly included officials from several other Arab countries. Saudi Arabia, which appeared close to normalisation in 2023, continues to insist that it will not establish ties with Israel unless an independent Palestinian state is established. Israeli media reported on 16 October, however, that Trump believes Saudi-Israeli normalisation is "back on the table". Israel's i24 news quoted Trump saying that Israel has provided assistance to Riyadh in its ongoing war against the Houthis in Yemen. Why, then, would any Arab government contemplate engagement with Israel? Economic incentives, American pressure and security concerns undoubtedly help explain their calculations. Normalisation, cooperation and meetings with Israel also offer Israel important diplomatic cover. Netanyahu has repeatedly argued that the Abraham Accords constitute evidence that Arab leaders do not care about the Palestinian cause and that some Arab leaders support Israel's war on Gaza. What kind of peace can Arab governments expect from a state whose security doctrine treats neighbouring states' weakness as a strategic advantage? The Abraham Accords were sold as a pathway to regional peace. Six years later, Hayman's analysis of Israel's security doctrine raises the possibility that Arab governments seeking security through normalisation may instead be helping to undermine their own. Albania's Rama uses culture to artwash Israel's genocide and growing repression Submitted by Klodiana Millona on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 14:36 As protesters face rubber bullets in Tirana, Edi Rama's government invokes Albania's wartime protection of Jews to justify deeper ties with Israel Protesters in Tirana hold placards reading "Enough Rama" and "Stop promoting his art" outside the prime minister's office on 12 June 2026 (Adnan Beci/AFP) Off In May 2026, residents of Zvernec, near Vlora, woke to find a coastline they had long accessed freely enclosed by barbed wire. When one of them was dragged away by masked private security guards in front of Albanian police, who stood by without intervening, images of the incident spread quickly, sparking public anger . Protests have since spread across Albania and its diaspora, with demonstrations in Tirana continuing for more than four months. The movement, known as the Flamingo Revolution , takes its name from the pink flamingos of the Narta lagoon, a protected wetland being cleared for a multibillion-dollar luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump and backed by Prime Minister Edi Rama. Then, in October, the protests escalated. Student-led demonstrations in Tirana calling for Rama's resignation have been met with rubber bullets, water cannon and teargas since 13 October. By 18 October, 272 people , including 169 police officers, had been injured, according to Albania's health ministry. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Kushner's Affinity Partners, which promotes investment links between Israel and the Arab world, is linked to the resort in Albania, and Kushner is also involved in the " redevelopment " of Gaza "after" the genocide . Albania is also among the five countries preparing to deploy troops to Gaza as part of the US -led International Stabilization Force. Less than 10km from Zvernec, Israel's largest defence company , Elbit Systems, is revitalising the Albanian Aviation School in partnership with the controversial state-owned military company Kayo, as part of broader military cooperation. Holocaust museum protests Two kilometres further, in Vlora's old town, the Albanian Jewish Museum is being built, honouring Albanians who saved Jews during World War Two. The project has sparked sustained protests in Vlora, where citizens and activists oppose the establishment of the museum in the Ethnographic Museum, a building of national cultural significance. Their objections centre on two issues: the call for an embargo on Israel rather than the expansion of cultural ties amid its war against Palestinians , and the concern that the project overshadows local history in favour of the government's geopolitical and private interests. Memory is mobilised as a soft power tool to normalise genocide on the other side of the Mediterranean Opposition has extended beyond Vlora, with demonstrations also taking place in Tirana, including outside Albania's culture ministry. The Flamingo Revolution has argued that the Vlora museum reflects a broader pattern of cultural diplomacy driven by political interests rather than heritage preservation. This cross-section of Vlora shows how luxury resorts on one side of the shore, militarisation nearby and cultural diplomacy inland are intertwined, and how memory is mobilised as a soft power tool to normalise genocide on the other side of the Mediterranean. States have long used culture , art and heritage to project moral legitimacy while pursuing their strategic interests. Israel has long invested in soft power, but it experienced a significant decline in the 2025 Global Soft Power Index, alongside a rise in boycotts and protests targeting its cultural institutions worldwide. Improving its reputation is therefore a high priority. Cultural initiatives and funding have intensified to enhance its international image , alongside artwashing that aims to deflect attention from or legitimise state violence. ‘The right to stay’: Italy’s Albanian diaspora sails back to support the Flamingo Revolution Read More » Intensified cultural ties with Albania offer Israel symbolic affirmation amid global criticism, while allowing the Albanian government to present its alignment as historically and morally grounded. Bilateral cooperation between Israel and Albania acquired greater political salience after October 2023. As Israel faced growing international protest, boycotts and diplomatic and legal scrutiny, Albania expanded cultural, memorial, educational and tourism cooperation. The memory of Albania's rescue of Jews during the Holocaust, increasingly articulated through the concept of besa, an Albanian code of honour, was central to this expansion. Until recently, Holocaust memory in Albania had not developed institutional frameworks comparable to those elsewhere in Eastern Europe. The story of Albanians protecting Jews through the cultural code of besa was usually invoked more as a patriotic-cum-cultural narrative than as a subject of rigorous historical engagement. Once peripheral to global Holocaust memory, Albania is now emerging as a newly "discovered" site for commemoration. Following the collapse of state socialism, the story of Albanians' protection of Jews was rediscovered and elevated as evidence of Albania's European moral credentials. Holocaust memory as diplomacy Albania's rescue narrative has been materialised through museums, memorials, street renamings, educational programmes and cooperation with Israeli and transnational Holocaust institutions. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Solomon Museum opened in Berat in 2018 and the Holocaust Memorial in Tirana in 2020, and Jews' Alley in Vlora has been incorporated into Albania's heritage landscape. Two new museums dedicated to the history of Albanian protection of Jews have also been announced. The Besa Museum in Tirana is funded by the Israeli philanthropist Alexander Machkevitch in collaboration with the culture ministry and designed by Oppenheim Architecture. The Albanian Jewish Museum in Vlora is funded by the Albanian-American Development Foundation and designed by Tel Aviv-based architects. Kushner's island land grab: Albanians are revolting against a system, not a resort Read More » Descendants of Jewish families once sheltered by Albanian households have taken part in commemorative projects that transform sites of refuge into places of remembrance and tourism. The " Qarrishta for the Jews " project, for example, commemorates the Bicaku family's sheltering of 26 Jews, combining a memorial site with guided tours, hiking and re-enactments of besa-based hospitality. The repeated invocation of besa is significant. An ethical obligation under Albanian customary law to protect a guest at all costs, besa has become a privileged explanatory device for Albanian exceptionalism during the Holocaust. Its contemporary mobilisation risks transforming a historically and socially situated practice into a political tool, presenting Albania's wartime protection of Jews as an enduring moral bond with Israel. The conflation of Jews as a historical and religious community with Israelis as citizens of a contemporary state is especially revealing. In Albanian, the word izraelit can mean both Israelite, an older term for Jews, and Israeli, which makes the slippage easy. Josef Jakoel's history of Albania's Jews, Izraelitet ne Shqiperi , written in the late 1980s and published in Albanian in 2020, uses izraelit in its older sense . Yet an English-language account of the book renders its title as "Israelis in Albania" and the Jakoels as an "Israeli family". Such slippage retrospectively nationalises Jewish victims as Israeli subjects and subtly transforms the memory of rescuing Jews into a narrative of historical affinity with the state of Israel. Culture as cover The rescue narrative is reinforced through educational and cultural programming, including teacher training , exhibitions and conferences framed around antisemitism prevention and "never again" discourses. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); These initiatives appear to align Holocaust remembrance with foreign policy priorities rather than respond to an established local problem. Albania has no significant history of antisemitism, a point celebrated by Israeli writers who heartily promote the country for tourism. Even the planned Albanian Jewish Museum states : "There has never been any trace of discrimination against Jews in Albania." Since October 2023, Israeli-sponsored exhibitions , book launches , film screenings , lectures and cultural weeks have multiplied in Tirana, often hosted in central and symbolic state-adjacent venues. These activities, together with sponsored visits to Israel for Albanian journalists, projected an image of cultural normality and mutual appreciation at a moment when Israeli cultural institutions elsewhere faced cancellations, protests and boycott campaigns . Tourism extended this normalisation. The launch of direct flights between Tel Aviv and Tirana in April 2025 was staged as a high-level diplomatic event . Rama welcomed the inaugural passengers at the Palace of Brigades, alongside senior ministers, Israeli tour operators, journalists and social media influencers, framing Albania as a safe and welcoming Muslim-majority destination. Rama, an artist himself, has often instrumentalised cultural projects as part of a broader strategy of artwashing , using museums, architectural spectacles and cultural branding to project Albania as a modern, tolerant and pro-western country. This strategy has helped him consolidate political power by shaping international perceptions, attracting foreign attention and deflecting criticism of democratic backsliding and outright authoritarian practices. Dissent is portrayed as anti-modern, parochial or hostile to development. Critics of such projects are frequently marginalised or delegitimised, cast as obstacles to Albania's inevitable integration into global circuits of capital and culture. Faced with the October protests, Rama blamed a "foreign hand". This model allows the government to aestheticise politics while deflecting attention from its own authoritarian practices and corruption. Selective memory The hypocrisy of the government's professed commitment to fighting antisemitism was starkest in July when, at the height of the Flamingo Revolution, it allocated 4m euros ($4.5m) in public funds for a custom-built stadium to host Kanye West (Ye), despite his open antisemitic declarations. Rama said the money was spent "to avoid embarrassing Albania in the eyes of nearly 25,000 foreign visitors". It was yet another attempt to portray the protesters as backward, unable to see Albania's supposed destiny as a centre of the music world. Albania's wartime protection of Jews is presented as an enduring moral bond with Israel We began in Vlora, where barbed wire cut off a coastline residents had always known as open, and where a fenced lagoon, a militarised aviation school and a museum honouring Albania's rescue of Jews sit within a few kilometres of one another, compressed into a single stretch of shore. Vlora also offers a counterpoint. On 21 August, three boats from the Global Sumud Flotilla arrived at the city's port, retracing in reverse the Adriatic crossing made 35 years earlier by the cargo ship Vlora to Bari, in Italy . The 1991 exodus remains etched into Albanian memory. Where the government's cultural diplomacy selectively remembers besa as an inherited bond with the state of Israel, the flotilla's arrival recalled a different, older solidarity , one that linked Albania's own history of flight and refuge to the Palestinian struggle for the right to return to the land. In the same city where the fences went up, that arrival stood as a quiet refusal: a reminder that memory, like the coastline itself, is still being contested, and that whoever controls its telling controls far more than the past. Judicial commission points finger at police’s ‘epic failure’, says Mir Raza was murdered. KARACHI: A judicial commission formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in businessman Mir Raza Ali’s murder case has pointed out the police’s “epic failure” in their investigation. The Sindh cabinet decided to make the report public during a meeting chaired by Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah earlier in the day. The judicial commission, which began its proceedings on Aug 28, held regular hearings to record statements of several individuals linked to the case. “ This case demonstrates an epic failure by the police in their investigation ,” declared the 62-page report submitted by Sindh High Court’s (SHC) Justice Omar Sial, who had been heading the judicial panel. “The police breached all required procedures, both knowingly and unknowingly, necessary to withstand judicial scrutiny and a successful prosecution,” the report stated. While acknowledging that the initial police response when they were informed of the presence of a body was prompt, the report noted that subsequent events “left a lot to be desired”. “It was a murder,” the report declared. It explained that the bullet trajectory, the unusual location of the wound if it had been a self-inflicted injury, the “absence of blood, the state of the body, the principles of medical jurisprudence, acid burns and the anaesthesia detected in the blood all clearly excluded suicide as the cause of death”. The commission determined that releasing the police findings before a proper investigation was “premature and fell short of professional standards”. “Even if the death had been a suicide, the police should have established who was responsible for driving a young man to that point, including whether coercion, blackmail, or instigation was involved. They made no such effort.” It said the police investigation “failed in its most basic duty: to establish the truth” . It further observed that “incessant public criticism of the police created problems” as the police “went into a shell, completely broke down communication channels, and took a position based on ego rather than on cogent, solid reasons”. The report pointed out specific issues with the police conduct: “Lack of leadership, seriousness, and supervision, and, in some cases, negligence by the senior officers. The handling of this case has been like a rudderless ship, not aware of its destination. “Ranging from negligent to criminally negligent, inexplicable, casual, and unprofessional investigation.” According to the commission, an active cover-up in the initial stages of the investigation cannot be conclusively ruled out . It noted that senior police officers swept clear investigative lapses under the carpet, without acknowledging them, addressing them, or even attempting to do so. “Too many cooks spoil the broth. The proverb is applicable to this case as far as the police are concerned,” the judicial commission observed. “Dozens of police officers – authorised and unauthorised – were involved in collecting evidence in this case, approaching and interrogating crucial persons, and in most cases not documenting it in any manner,” it said, adding that therefore, no officer was willing to take responsibility for the lapses . The inquiry said there was a need to mitigate public speculation by an “honest and timely briefing on the investigation”, but this was not done, and the family or the public were not updated through official disclosures. “The police did not follow the commission’s recommendation to appoint a focal person for this reason. As a result, public speculation further embarrassed the government and the police.” Regarding the controversy over the reconstitution of a medical board formed for the exhumation of Ali’s body, the report said: “The overnight bureaucratic manoeuvring was a highly irregular, inexplicable, legally flawed overreach dictated entirely from the upper echelons of the Sindh Health Secretariat, more specifically by the secretary and special secretary, Health.” It added that the Health Services director general , “being aware that he was not legally competent to form a medical board for exhumation, looked the other way”. “The two gentlemen who directed the change in the board could not give a cogent reason for the abrupt change, making it extremely controversial, fueling public speculation, and embarrassing the Sindh government.” Referring to an Aug 9 meeting held at CM House, which “drew considerable speculation and controversy”, the report said that “no ulterior motive can be inferred from this meeting”. The meeting was attended by Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) Dr Osama Sheikh, who conducted Ali’s first autopsy, the Karachi police chief and other senior officials. Observations on officials Listing its observations for certain police officials involved in the case, the judicial panel identified “criminal negligence” on the part of Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal of Ferozabad police station. “Initiate a comprehensive inquiry into him, leading to dismissal from service. He should be suspended in the interim. He must also be questioned to determine whether he has facilitated the destruction of key evidence,” the report read. It said that the person Mushtaq named as his source did not corroborate the information he provided, raising suspicion regarding his conduct. It further said that the WhatsApp messages Ali sent to Sarim Bin Tahir asking for Rs30m, which was “full of uncharacteristic grammatical errors and truncated spellings and read as acute panic”, suggested the deceased was being “blackmailed or threatened”. It also noted that while CCTV footage showed Ali with a pistol on the night he was killed, this was “unusual”. “All his close friends and associates told the Commission that Raza did not possess or use pistols. They said he would probably not even know how to handle one. Witnesses also vouched for his peace-loving, calm, and gentle demeanour. Why he took the pistol remained a mystery. The pistol, however, has not been found to date,” it said. It further said: “The known financial distress was also not of such a nature that would lead a person to suicide. Ali’s behaviour, until the ride-hailing service dropped him off, did not suggest he was ready to take an extreme step for this reason.” Recommendations Suggesting the next steps, the judicial commission said accommodating the family’s request for a joint investigation team (JIT) was the “most viable path to mitigate ongoing reputational damage to the Government of Sindh”. It recommended that a JIT be constituted under the leadership of Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Irfan Baloch to “balance the need for public accountability with preserving Sindh Police morale and reputation”. The report said the team should “integrate senior representatives from the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Intelligence Bureau (IB), Pakistan Rangers (Sindh), and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to ensure an impartial, comprehensive, and credible resolution. “This extreme step is necessary to restore public trust and end speculation,” it stressed. The report pointed out that the case could now “only be resolved through a rigorous, intelligence-based investigation as a “significant portion of physical evidence has been compromised” . It called for the police to “transparently acknowledge and apologise for past operational lapses”, as well as immediately initiate formal inquiries against the responsible officers in light of the report. While stating that it did not have investigative powers and that it was difficult to conclude conclusively that an active cover-up occurred, the commission noted that “certain inexplicable actions are difficult to justify and raise the possibility that one may have occurred”. Therefore, it suggested that a high-level committee, preferably led by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), be constituted to initiate criminal action against any police officials it finds culpable. The committee would inquire into “whether any of the police officials involved in this probe in the first 10 days” were in breach of sections 201 (causing disappearance of evidence of offence), 166(2) (public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury) and 218 (public servant framing incorrect record or writing with intent to save person from punishment) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). The judicial commission also called for initiating police reforms, particularly to address and modernise the investigation protocol. It suggested forming a committee of “seasoned professionals” to “specifically address first response, crime scene handling, medico-legal dynamics, collection, safekeeping, and analysis of evidence, and recording the entirety of the investigation in written or digital form”. While it proposed a three-month timeframe for the exercise, the commission said the Sindh government will make the final decision. Another suggestion was to consider an increase in the investigation budget, with a protocol in place to monitor the fund’s use. The panel further suggested steps regarding training of investigators and enhancing the capacity of Crime Scene Units. Panel formed to ensure implementation The judicial panel’s primary mandate was to determine the facts and circumstances of the case; assess whether police and medico-legal investigations were impartial; identify professional negligence, misconduct, evidence manipulation, or cover-ups; review digital/forensic evidence; and recommend further investigation, forensic analysis, or legal/departmental action. According to a handout issued by the Sindh chief minister’s spokesperson, the judicial inquiry report was presented in seven separate sealed envelopes. It will be uploaded on the website of the provincial home department on Tuesday, while a copy will also be provided to the aggrieved family. Further, CM Shah also constituted a three-member sub-committee to ensure the implementation of the report. According to a notification issued by the Sindh government, the committee comprises Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar as convener, Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah and Labour Minister Saeed Ghani. The Sindh advocate general will provide legal assistance to the committee and the additional chief secretary of the Home department will provide secretarial support, the notification said. The committee will oversee the implementation of the commission’s findings and will submit its recommendations to the Sindh chief minister “at the earliest”, and present them before the Cabinet in its next meeting, it added. Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon also took to X to announce that the report would be made public on Tuesday. “The government of Sindh remains committed to transparency, accountability and ensuring that due process of law is upheld,” he said. Last week, the commission handed over the sealed report to the provincial government after examining 49 witnesses during 15 hearings. The inquiry report, along with associated documents, was handed over to the focal person of the provincial government and Home Department Additional Secretary Javed Ahmed Abro by the commission registrar, Abdul Majid, on the premises of the SHC. After receiving the record, Abro told reporters that he would hand over the sealed report along with other records to the provincial government and it was the prerogative of the government to decide whether the inquiry report was to be brought into the public domain or otherwise. In August, the provincial government formed the commission, which was tasked with making recommendations for further investigation and forensic analysis or legal/departmental action, and it was required to submit its findings and recommendations to the Sindh government within 30 days. However, the commission had struggled to meet its deadline and sent an application last month to the Sindh government for an extension in its tenure till Oct 15. Therefore, the provincial cabinet granted an extension. Besides examining 49 witnesses and available record, the commission had also sent questionnaires to Karachi police chief Azad Khan, head of current investigation team DIG Amir Farooqui and DIG East Farrukh Lanjar after dismissing an application by the aggrieved family to summon the senior police officers to testify before the commission. The 25-year-old businessman and Institute of Business Administration graduate had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS and his body with gunshot wounds was found a day later in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar’s locality. Initially, the police built the case around suicide on the basis of the first autopsy , which indicated a bullet entry wound on the chest, and by pointing out business losses and money borrowed by the victim. Police surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had disputed the findings of the first post-mortem conducted by medico-legal officer Dr Osama Sheikh. The second post-mortem report termed the findings of the first report “inconsistent” with suicide as the manner of Mir Raza’s death. It said the Exhumation Board was of the unanimous opinion that the death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back. Additional input by Tahir Siddiqui
