Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs382.02 per litre while HSD will cost Rs389.80 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 21 (Wednesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

State of deceased’s eyes not proof of ‘unwitnessed’ death: SC. • Court dismisses petitions challenging double-murder convictions • Verdict explains that closing eyes of a corpse is ‘religious’ custom, not legal duty ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that the condition of a deceased person’s eyes at the time of death cannot conclusively establish the fact that the incident was not witnessed. The Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, 1984, does not impose a legal duty to close a deceased person’s eyes. Rather, the practice is customary and religious, observed Justice Salahuddin Panhwar while dismissing jail petitions filed by Azmat Ullah alias Motu and Muhammad Luqman alias Gona. The petitioners had challenged their convictions in a 2011 double-murder case, upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) on May 18, 2022. Justice Panhwar was part of a three-member bench, headed by Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar. The bench upheld the convictions under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code but maintained the high court’s decision to commute the death sentences to life imprisonment. In criminal trials, defence lawyers often argue that an incident was ‘unwitnessed’ if the post-mortem report records the deceased’s eyes as open, reasoning that close relatives would ordinarily close them after death. During the hearing, the petitioners’ counsel pointed to discrepancies in eyewitness statements and argued that the post-mortem and inquest reports, which recorded the eyes of both victims as open, indicated that the murders had not been witnessed. Article 129 versus rigid presumptions In a nine-page judgement, Justice Panhwar referred to Article 129 of the Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, which allows courts to presume facts they consider likely in the circumstances of a particular case. However, the judgement stressed that human behaviour could not be assessed in a vacuum or through rigid assumptions. Responses to trauma, terror and violent loss vary from person to person, making it unsafe to draw categorical conclusions from a single circumstance. It noted that relatives witnessing a gruesome incident may be overwhelmed by shock and trauma. Hoping their loved one might survive, they may focus on obtaining urgent medical assistance rather than performing customary rituals associated with death. Relatives and bystanders may also continue treating the victim as injured until a doctor or police official confirms death, which may not be immediately apparent at the scene. Other factors From a forensic perspective, the position of the eyelids is governed by physiological processes rather than the presence or absence of witnesses, the judgement explained. Following death, muscles initially become relaxed, allowing eyelids to remain open or partially open, a condition known as lagophthalmos. Handling or moving a body may also cause previously closed eyes to reopen, particularly before rigor mortis develops. As rigor mortis sets in, muscles become stiff and retain their prevailing position. The court also cited Locard’s Exchange Principle, which holds that every contact leaves a trace. Relatives, bystanders and rescue workers may avoid touching a body to prevent contamination or disturbance of blood-spatter patterns, trace evidence and DNA material before forensic experts arrive. It would therefore be unsafe to presume that every person knows how to handle a deceased body or feels obliged to close the eyes, the judgement said. Concluding that neither forensic literature nor the law recognises closed eyes as an indicator of a witnessed death, the court rejected the argument that open eyelids alone could establish that a crime was unwitnessed. The judgement further observed that minor discrepancies and natural variations in eyewitness accounts, arising from the passage of time and the rigours of cross-examination, do not undermine otherwise credible and consistent testimony. Balochistan says Rs14bn spent to counter terrorism. • Insists 18 laws enacted, 17 institutions set up under security plans • Officials claim 60,000 operations conducted, 1,100 terrorists killed QUETTA: The Balochistan government has passed 18 laws, established 17 institutions and departments and spent more than Rs14 billion on counterterrorism measures under the National Action Plan, Counterterrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan, senior provincial officials said on Tuesday. They also claimed that more than 60,000 counterterrorism operations had been conducted across Balochistan up to October, killing over 1,000 terrorists. The Counter-Terrorism Depart­ment alone had killed 250 terrorists and arrested another 250 suspects. They said 101 police personnel and around 200 members of other law enforcement agencies had lost their lives, while 551 civilians had been killed in terrorist violence. The figures were revealed during a joint press conference held by Provincial Home Minister Ziaullah Langove along with Chief Mini­ster’s Adviser on Media and Political Aff­a­irs Shahid Rind and Additional Chief Secretary Home Hamza Shafqaat. They said measures had also been taken to secure the Quetta-Rakhni, Quetta-Karachi and Quetta-Taftan highways and expressed confidence that the security situation would improve over the next three to four months. Mr Shafqaat said the provincial government had taken a series of measures over the past two years to implement the National Action Plan, Counter Terrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan. IMF urges Pakistan to move beyond fiscal targets. ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has called for Pakistan’s fiscal policy to go beyond achieving primary balance targets and protecting debt sustainability by reinforcing policy credibility, fostering economic recovery and creating space for public investment and social spending to support stronger long-term growth. Speaking at a workshop on “Reforms for a Modern and Growth-Friendly Tax System in Pakistan”, IMF Middle East and Central Asia Department Director Jihad Azour said tax refo­rm was critical to Pak­is­tan’s economic growth agenda and rema­ined central to the objectives of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF). The workshop was organised by the Ministry of Finance and Revenue in collaboration with the IMF. Finance Minister Muha­mmad Aurangzeb also spoke at the workshop, highlighting achiev­ements over the past two years. Mr Azour said Pakistan had made important progress towards restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding confidence, strengthening external buffers and supporting a gradual economic recovery despite an era of shocks and uncertainty. Jihad Azour calls for broader, more predictable tax system The IMF official said Pakistan’s recent stabilisation gains had created an opportunity that needed to be strengthened through transformative reforms, with tax reform at the heart of the process. “A stronger, broader, fairer and more predictable tax system can support fiscal sustainability while reducing distortions that hold back investment, productivity, growth and formal job creation,” he remarked. He said broadening the tax base, strengthening revenue administration, reducing tax expenditures, protecting priority spending and improving public service provision were Pakistan’s priorities. He credited Pakistan for the progress made. However, he said the next milestone was to turn stabilisation into stronger and more durable growth by moving beyond cycles of adjustment towa­r­ds a more competitive, inv­e­s­tment-friendly and inclusive economy. Mr Azour said the IMF remained committed to supporting the authorities in building an economy capable of delivering hig­her productivity, led by a stronger private sector, and creating better opportunities for younger generations. He warned that the highly uncertain external environment had made these objectives more urgent. Fiscal policy, he said, must do more than achieve primary balance targets and protect debt sustainability. It must reinforce policy credibility, foster recovery and create space for public investment and social spending needed to support long-term growth and public welfare. Outlining four themes for discussion during the two-day workshop, Mr Azour identified credibility, growth, fairness and implementation as central to the reform process. Draft auto policy sent to cabinet. ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday approved the draft Auto Policy 2026-31, which aims to increase auto sector exports to $6 billion and boost local production, competitiveness and electric vehicle (EV) adoption. Although the Prime Minister’s Office did not issue an official statement, sources in the federal government shared the final draft, which was presented to the premier by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Adviser on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar. The draft policy will be presented to the federal cabinet for in-principle approval, then it will need parliament’s nod. The policy aims to bring the auto sector to open competition by significantly reducing tariffs on completely built-up units (CBUs) and completely knocked-down (CKD) kits up to 15pc by 2030-31. PM ‘okays’ five-year roadmap; policy targets $6bn exports, tariff cuts by 2031; proposes 1pc sales tax on EVs Under the proposed draft, battery electric vehicles will be subject to a 1pc sales tax during 2026-31. The document proposes a 6pc sales tax on range-extended electric vehicles and a 9pc on plug-in hybrid vehicles. A 10pc federal excise duty has been proposed on electric vehicles valued more than $75,000. The policy also envisages lower tariffs on smaller electric vehicles priced below $15,000. To encourage EV adoption, the government has approved proposals to raise the financing limit from Rs3 million to Rs10m and extend the repayment period from three to five years, making smaller vehicles more affordable for low-income consumers. The government has set the total export target of $6.01bn during the five years of the policy, which includes combined exports of parts and vehicles amounting to $256.6m for 2026-27, $671.8m for 2027-28, $1.11bn for 2028-29, $1.17bn for 2029-30 and $2.19bn for 2030-31 the fifth year of the auto policy. The policy also proposes mandatory export targets for vehicle manufacturers, with incentives for companies that increase exports. Under the proposed incentive mechanism, manufacturers would receive compensation equivalent to 5pc of export value for boosting exports, along with an additional 10pc incentive on exports exceeding the previous year’s level. Companies that fail to meet their export targets would face penalties, and manufacturing certificates could be cancelled if targets remain unmet for two consecutive years. The policy also sets new targets to increase the use of locally manufactured auto parts. Companies failing to meet local production targets could lose their incentives. The government expects to collect more than Rs232bn through the Automotive Development Levy over five years. The proceeds would be used to finance export incentives and industrial development programmes, including funding for technology upgrades by auto parts manufacturers. The policy proposes levying the Automotive Development Levy on vehicles with engine capacities exceeding 1,000cc. To strengthen quality assurance and regulatory oversight, the government plans to establish the Pakistan Automotive Testing Institute. The policy also provides funding for research, certification, and third-party audits, as well as the adoption of international safety standards for locally manufactured and imported vehicles. Meanwhile, Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (Paapam) Chairman Abdul Rehman Aizaz said the new policy, by lowering the import tariff on parts to 15pc, would phase out local parts manufacturers and benefit assemblers, warning that assemblers could eventually be phased out as imported cars take over.“This policy will make Pakistan an import destination country with no local industrial base in the auto sector,” he remarked. CDF Munir-Pezeshkian meeting raises peace hopes. ISLAMABAD: Iranian leaders have told Pakistan that the United States must take the first steps to rebuild trust, and that the acceptance of Tehran’s seven-point proposal could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations. The message was conveyed during Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s visit on Tuesday, where he met with President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s supreme leader and secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also accompanied the army chief. As diplomatic efforts intensified to prevent a resumption of hostilities, Field Marshal Munir’s visit is being viewed as a move to quell escalating regional tensions. Tehran says acceptance of its 7-point proposal can be starting point for renewed talks with US The visit came a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks with Iranian leaders on the conflict and efforts to restore regional stability. The visit was aimed at conveying messages and exploring whether the Islamabad understanding could still provide a basis for negotiations, but no breakthrough or formal agreement was announced after Tuesday’s meetings. The discussions also touched on bilateral relations, including a recent disruption in commercial trade across the Pakistan-Iran border. Iranian officials also raised concerns over the closure, while Field Marshal Munir told them that the border closure was temporary and due to technical reasons and that the crossings had reopened on Tuesday. Importantly, Iranian officials reportedly shared with the field marshal their response to a US proposal, reiterating that Tehran would not make concessions under pressure and that Washington must meet its conditions before trust could be restored. While there was no official word from Pakistan’s Foreign Office or Inter-Services Public Relations, Iranian media described the response as “clear, serious, and explicit”. An Iranian source said the visiting Pakistani army chief was told that “Iran has nothing new to say to the Americans” and it was for them to return to Islamabad Memorandum. Although not many details about President Pezeshkian’s meeting were released to media, in a post that was unrelated to his meeting with Field Marshal Munir, the president said that Iranians may endure hardship, but they will not surrender their land. Speaker Ghalibaf told Field Marshal Munir that the US could not regain Iran’s trust without fulfilling the seven conditions Tehran had presented during meetings in New York. He said Washington’s past actions, including what Iran considers a violation of the Islamabad understanding, had only deepened its distrust of the US administration. “Threats and military manoeuvres cannot influence the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Mr Ghalibaf said, according to an Iranian account of the meeting, adding that it was now up to Washington to take the necessary steps to extricate itself from the conflict. Mr Rezaei, meanwhile, said Iran would not surrender its enriched nuclear material, describing it as a national asset intended for domestic use. He said Iranian officials were united in their view that negotiations could not proceed without steps by Washington to meet Tehran’s conditions. The inflexible Iranian response has thrown a challenge for Pakistan, which has sought to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran after an earlier diplomatic breakthrough failed to produce a lasting settlement. Islamabad brokered a ceasefire in April and hosted direct talks that led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June. The agreement outlined steps towards easing the conflict, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic and nuclear issues, but the process subsequently stalled after disagreements. Despite the breakdown of the peace process, Pakistan has continued to offer its good offices to both sides for preventing another round of fighting. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

Makkah alliance binds partners to decade-long pact. • Turkiye seeks parliamentary nod for defence agreement; officials say Ankara’s support may be limited to provision of weapons, equipment and intelligence sharing • Pakistan has already ratified treaty; only PM and cabinet’s nod required under Article 90 • Egypt’s parliament to vote on support for Riyadh on Oct 26 • Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia expected to sign defence cooperation agreement in Doha today ANKARA: Turkiye has submitted the Makkah defence pact to parliament for ratification, moving Nato’s second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it continues to face Houthi attacks. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The provision, similar to Nato’s Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attacks. All three members have agreed to use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, as per the text seen by Reuters. The agreement will enter into force upon the deposit of the ratification documents with the secretariat in Riyadh, and will remain valid indefinitely. The parties may not withdraw from the agreement for the first 10 years. While Pakistan has made it clear that ‘collective deterrence measures’ under the trilateral defence agreement are “already in play”, Ankara still requires formal parliamentary ratification for the agreement. According to official sources, Pakistan follows an executive-led treaty-making system, where the federal government’s ratification is enough for subjects in the federal legislative list. According to Article 90 of the Constitution, “the executive authority of the Federation shall be exercised in the name of the President by the Federal Government, consisting of the Prime Minister and the Federal Ministers, which shall act through the Prime Minister, who shall be the chief executive of the Federation.” However, under Tur­kiye’s constitution, separate permission from parliament is required to deploy troops abroad, regardless of any international agreement. According to the Reuters news agency, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtu­lmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, is expected to refer the agreement to parliament’s foreign affairs commission upon his ret­urn, which could debate the agreement as early as Friday. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s communications director, Burha­nettin Dur­an, said that Turk­iye’s re­cent step marked an important mile­stone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations. “This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to stre­ngthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region,” Duran said in a post on X. A Turkish official, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity, said Turkiye’s own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far. Asked how Turkiye could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Makkah Agree­ment was not an “offensive agreement,” adding that Turkiye would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory. Although not part of the Makkah alliance, Egypt’s parliament is also expe­cted to vote on authorising pote­ntial military support for Saudi Arabia on Oct 26. Ahead of its submission for parliamentary appr­oval, the contents of the agreement were published in full for the first time by Turkish state broadcaster, TRT Haber. Turkiye, which has a rob­ust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh’s military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against “all means of terrorism,” including at the operational level. Defence deal Meanwhile, TRT World also reported that Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia are expected to sign a defence industry cooperation memorandum today (Wednesday). The signing will be held in Qatar, which is also expected to announce plans to establish a local defence production hub, the Gulf state’s Minister of State for Defence Affairs Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday. Turkish Defence Mini­ster Yasar Guler will travel to Doha for the signing. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who was also in Doha for the security for­um , is expected to represent Pakistan at the signing. Earlier, Mr Naqvi met with his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, who also commands Qatar’s Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya). The two discussed the current regional situation and matters concerning regional peace and stability, the state-run APP news agency reported. During their meeting, the two men agreed to expand the security partnership between Pakistan and Qatar. They also held detailed discussions on expanding cooperation in areas related to internal security. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s transfer-only policy for IHC judges challenged. ISLAMABAD: A writ petition filed in the Islamabad High Court has challenged the Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s (JCP) April 28 decision that vacancies arising from the transfer of a judge “shall be filled through transfer only”, arguing that the three vacant judges’ seats in the IHC should be filled through fresh appointments under the Constitution rather than further transfers. The petition, filed by Advocate Supreme Court Syed Nayyab Hassan Gardezi against the Federation of Pakistan, JCP, president and prime minister, contends that the impugned decision has no constitutional foundation and conflicts with Article 175A(8), which requires the commission to nominate one person “for each vacancy” of a high court judge. It argues that the Constitution recognises no category of high court vacancy exempt from this requirement and that the commission cannot create one through a resolution. The petition contends that the JCP decision was taken in disregard of the procedure prescribed by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (Appointment of Judges) Rules 2024. It points out that Rule 11(2) requires the secretary to notify all members at least 14 days before a scheduled meeting, providing the agenda and supporting materials. According to the petition, the impugned decision was reportedly introduced during the proceedings rather than being included in the circulated agenda. It further states that the JCP Rules, as notified, contain no provision for their amendment, while the only provision allowing the commission to remove difficulties — Rule 15 — requires the votes of at least two-thirds of its total membership. The impugned decision, however, records only a “majority of its total membership”. The petition also questions the composition of the JCP when the decision was taken. It argues that the impugned decision governs future appointments to the IHC, yet it was taken at meetings convened to consider transfers, at which the commission sat under the first proviso to Article 200(1), with the chief justices of the high courts concerned in each transfer. By contrast, the Constitution prescribes a distinct composition for the appointment of IHC judges under Article 175A(6). Besides the IHC chief justice, it includes the head of IHC’s constitutional benches, an advocate nominated by the Islamabad Bar Council and a federal minister nominated by the prime minister. The petitioner submits that procedural and compositional defects reinforce the need for the IHC’s three vacancies, created by the transfers notified on April 29, 2026, to be filled through the constitutional process of fresh appointments. For this purpose, nominations should be invited from members of the commission under Article 175A(23) and Rule 9(1) of the JCP Rules, rather than through a transfer-only route. The petition also challenges the decision on grounds of discrimination, retrospectivity and an unlawful fetter on discretion. It notes that in July 2026, the JCP filled vacancies in the Lahore High Court, Sindh High Court and Baloc­histan High Court through initial appointments, while the IHC’s vacancies have been reserved for transfers. It emphasises that the IHC is currently functioning with a chief justice and nine judges against a sanctioned strength of a chief justice and 12 judges, and that the three vacancies have remained unfilled for more than five months. Along with the writ petition, the petitioner has filed an application for interim relief, seeking to restrain the respondents from recommending, advising or notifying the transfer of any judge to the IHC against the three vacancies while the petition remains pending. The petition seeks a declaration that the JCP’s decision is ultra vires Articles 4, 25, 175A and 193 of the Constitution and the JCP Rules, and is of no legal effect. Pakistan warns India against attempt to alter strategic balance. ISLAMABAD: Adviser to the National Command Authority retired Lt Gen Khalid Kidwai on Tuesday warned that Pakistan could review its deployment options to restore strategic balance in South Asia, saying India was moving towards a more prepared, potentially first-use capable nuclear posture. “Pakistan never has and never will accept strategic imbalances to be induced in South Asia,” Mr Kidwai said at the second Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference, hosted by the Strategic Vision Institute, an Islamabad based think tank specialising in strategic issues. “Pakistan will review and reconsider all options for appropriate deployments in order to restore the strategic balance and strategic stability while retaining the policy of strategic ambiguity,” he added. Mr Kidwai and retired Lt Gen Sarfraz Sattar, both former heads of the Strategic Plans Division and advisers to the NCA, said India’s reported deployment of nuclear weapons aboard a submarine, alongside missile modernisation and recent military confrontations, raised the risk of escalation between the two neighbouring arch rivals. NCA adviser reminds India of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy Nuclear warheads Citing the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s SIPRI Yearbook 2026 and other publicly available information, they pointed to reports that India had deployed around 12 nuclear warheads on a submarine for deterrence patrols. They also cited missile canisterisation and wider nuclear and conventional modernisation as developments that cast doubt on India’s declared No-First-Use policy. Mr Kidwai said the reported deployment suggested India had mated nuclear warheads with submarine launched ballistic missiles and begun sea based deterrence patrols. “I do not see any reason as to why an SIPRI report might be inaccurate or speculative,” he said. “This irresponsible escalatory transition towards creating asymmetry in nuclear posture will have profound destabilising effects on South Asian strategic stability,” he added. Mr Kidwai said India’s ability to maintain a continuous at sea deterrent further undermined the credibility of its No-First-Use policy and pointed to a more offensive nuclear posture. “The operational reality that emerges is that India can undertake a first strike against Pakistan at zero notice,” he said. Advance notification He also questioned the absence of advance notification for Indian submarine launched ballistic missile tests, warning that such developments could heighten the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. Referring to the February 2019 confrontation, he said India had reportedly deployed its Arihant nuclear submarine in the Indian Ocean after carrying out air strikes near Balakot in Pakistan, presumably with nuclear weapons aboard. He described the latest reported deployment as part of India’s wider effort to operationalise mated nuclear weapons on submarines. “Pakistan reserves the right to undertake all appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and preserve strategic balance in the region under all circumstances,” Mr Kidwai said. He urged India to understand the implications of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy. “India in fact will be well advised to read and re-read Pakistan’s policy of Full Spectrum Deterrence and seriously absorb its wide ranging implications for strategic deterrence, strategic stability, and for India’s security,” he said. Mr Sattar said the May 2025 conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbours showed how quickly conventional hostilities could escalate. The ceasefire came after both sides used cruise and ballistic missiles and India deployed strategic naval assets, he said. He drew parallels with the 2019 confrontation, when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to the deployment of nuclear submarines for deterrence patrols and the positioning of BrahMos missiles along Pakistan’s border. The May 2025 fighting was more intense, involving kamikaze drones, supersonic BrahMos missiles capable of carrying conventional or nuclear warheads, and cyber and electronic warfare, he said. “It is now clear that the 2025 conflict was much more lethal in comparison to the 2019 conflict,” Mr Sattar said, warning that the fighting risked spiralling towards nuclear escalation through accident or miscalculation. He cited India’s canisterisation of land and sea based missiles, pursuit of multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) capabilities, short-range tactical missiles, ballistic missile defences, hypersonic weapons and autonomous platforms as further sources of concern. Combined with India’s Cold Start doctrine, wider military modernisation and the absence of a bilateral arms control mechanism, these developments raised doubts about its No-First-Use declaration and traditionally recessed deterrence posture, he said. “Rather, as I said, it signals a shift towards more first use capable posture,” Mr Sattar said. “The future strategic stability in South Asia is placed on a perilous and worrisome course with heightened risk of misunderstanding and miscalculation, potentially leading to unintended or accidental escalation to the nuclear level,” he added. Hegseth discusses Iran with Netanyahu in unannounced visit. JERUSALEM: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived in Israel on an unannounced visit, and discussed the Iran war with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as tensions continue to simmer between the US and Iran. Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli PM, confirmed that Netanyahu had met Hegseth at the Uvda air force base in Israel’s southern Negev desert region. Mr Netanyahu and Mr Hegseth discussed “the threats in the region” and the US-Israel partnership in dealing both “offensively and defensively” with those threats, he said in a brief phone call. The defence secretary thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump’s support for the prime minister. Israeli PM celebrates Trump’s endorsement ahead of next week’s election “There’s a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion,” Spielman said. The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Mr Hegseth’s visit. Earlier, he posted that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia, but did not specify where he had met the personnel. Hegseth’s visit comes as tensions flare between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen’s Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Israeli prime minister also said he spoke with President Trump on Sunday about the importance of eliminating the Iranian government. “We are committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime,” Mr Netanyahu said in a statement released by his office. “I have discussed this with Trump many times, including the day before yesterday.” Netanyahu basks in Trump endorsement Netanyahu basked in Trump’s endorsement on Monday ahead of close-fought elections, airing a phone call in which the US president predicted he would win, and suggested they may again attack Iran together. “I think you’re going to have a tremendous victory, actually,” the US president can be heard saying on speakerphone. “You’re the man I want by my side, Bibi,” Donald Trump said, referring to Mr Netanyahu by his nickname. Netanyahu, while reminding the famously loose-lipped president that they were on an open line, hailed Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in February. “Donald, we have a job to finish,” Netanyahu beamed. “We’ll finish it together. We’ll finish it, and no one else will do it.” Netanyahu did not elaborate, but again described Iran as “the greatest danger”. Trump, 80, and Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Wednesday, have forged a close partnership at a time when both are vastly unpopular in public opinion in most democratic nations. The pair have also managed to avoid prosecution while in power, with Mr Netanyahu facing charges of corruption that could land him in prison. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

Prism Reflections: Why should we tell the FBR what the FBR already knows?. Why must taxpayers tell FBR what it already knows? body{margin:0;background:#FFFFFF} a{color:#0E7A43}a:hover{color:#095A31} .hl{background:#D4EEDD;color:#10331F;padding:1px 3px;border-radius:2px;-webkit-box-decoration-break:clone;box-decoration-break:clone} .rq{text-decoration:underline;text-decoration-color:#7B4BB7;text-decoration-thickness:3px;text-underline-offset:6px} .p{margin:0 0 26px} Imagine an ordinary taxpayer sitting before a computer on a Sunday morning. The salary certificate is beside her. Bank statements are ready. Details of property, vehicles and savings have been collected. Tax has already been deducted from salary and perhaps from numerous other transactions during the year. She knows what she earned, what she owns and, broadly, what she owes. Surely, she thinks, this should not take very long. She logs into IRIS. Two hours later, she is considerably less certain—not merely about the tax return, but almost about her own financial existence. That, unfortunately, appears to describe the experience of many taxpayers. Responses to my recent article on the time allowed for filing income tax returns were illuminating. One reader maintained that filing takes only a few minutes and questioned why taxpayers need months. Fair enough. For a person familiar with IRIS, possessing uncomplicated affairs and fortunate enough to encounter no technical difficulty, that may indeed be true. READ ALSO We were ready with our tax filings, was the FBR? However, another regular taxpayer reported trying unsuccessfully for two weeks and making 72 attempts to access the system. Others complained that amendments to one part of the return require revisiting connected sections; that increasingly minute details of assets and income are demanded; and that figures sometimes migrate from previous returns in ways taxpayers find difficult to correct. One particularly interesting comment came from a salaried taxpayer who asked a deceptively simple question: why should someone whose only income is salary, and whose tax has already been deducted at source, be required to negotiate a complicated annual exercise at all? These experiences may differ, but collectively they raise a question more important than whether IRIS is technically functional: For whom is the return actually designed? Tax administrators understandably think in terms of sections, codes, withholding categories, heads of income, adjustable taxes, wealth reconciliation and statutory declarations. Ordinary citizens do not. They think differently. I earned this much. My employer deducted this much tax. I have one house. I bought a car. I have money in two bank accounts. I sold nothing this year. I have no foreign income. Now tell me what you need. A genuinely taxpayer-friendly system should begin there. Suppose upon logging into IRIS, instead of confronting numerous tabs, codes and fields, taxpayers were welcomed with a few simple questions: Were you employed during the year? Did you receive income from any source other than salary? Did you carry on a business? Did you buy or sell property, shares or any other significant asset? Do you have foreign income or assets? Depending upon the answers, irrelevant portions of the return could simply disappear. Why should a salaried individual with one source of income navigate screens designed to accommodate business profits, complicated investments or multiple commercial activities? Conversely, a businessperson, association of persons or company would naturally be taken to the more detailed portions appropriate to its affairs. Simplification does not mean treating every taxpayer alike. It means asking each taxpayer only what is relevant to that taxpayer. The FBR already recognises this distinction to some extent. Its own guidance provides a separate declaration form for qualifying salaried persons, while IRIS remains the portal through which online returns are filed. The problem is that simplification should not merely exist as another form or menu. It should define the taxpayer's entire experience. There is an even more obvious possibility. Why should taxpayers repeatedly tell the FBR what the FBR already knows? FBR's own Maloomat (Information) portal acknowledges that it possesses third-party and internally generated information concerning withholding payments, properties, vehicles, travel, credit-card transactions, debit transactions and other financial activity. Existing taxpayers can access some of that information through IRIS. Then why not use it intelligently? A salaried taxpayer's employer has already reported deductions. Banks have reported withholding. Property and vehicle transactions increasingly leave electronic trails. Previous wealth statements sit within FBR's own system. Instead of asking: “Tell us everything again.” IRIS could say: “This is what we already have. Please confirm, correct or supplement it.” That single change would alter the psychology of tax compliance. Imagine opening your return and finding your salary and tax deducted already populated. Your previously declared assets appear alongside them. A vehicle purchased during the year is flagged for confirmation. Bank withholding is displayed. The system asks whether anything is missing. You review. You correct. You add what the FBR could not know. You submit. Technology would then be doing what technology is supposed to do: removing work rather than merely relocating bureaucracy from paper to screen. The FBR already requires wealth statements to reconcile mathematically before submission. Its own guidance states that a wealth statement cannot be successfully submitted unless the change in wealth corresponds with income and expenditure. That may serve a legitimate tax purpose, but the portal should help taxpayers understand why a difference exists rather than merely preventing submission. If the reconciliation fails by Rs. 200,000, the taxpayer should not have to wander through different screens searching for the missing figure. The system should say: Your declared wealth has increased by Rs. 200,000 more than the resources presently explained. Please check the following possible areas. That is guidance. A red error message is not. There is another misconception worth addressing. Making returns easier does not mean weakening tax enforcement. Quite the opposite. Complexity is the friend of neither compliance nor enforcement. It creates mistakes, dependence upon intermediaries and enormous quantities of unreliable data. An accurately completed simple return is considerably more useful than an elaborate return filled incorrectly because the taxpayer did not understand what was being asked. Sophisticated taxpayers with businesses, multiple income streams, capital transactions or corporate structures will continue to need detailed returns and professional advice. Tax practitioners will hardly become redundant. But should an educated salaried citizen with straightforward affairs need a tax consultant simply to tell the government what the government largely knows already? That should become the basic test of reform: Can an ordinary person with ordinary financial affairs file an accurate return without professional assistance? If not, we have digitized taxation without genuinely simplifying it. One reader responding to my earlier article put the problem in five words: “Digitization cannot change mindsets.” Precisely. A complicated bureaucracy transferred from files and registers onto a computer does not automatically become modern administration. At worst, it becomes electronic bureaucracy—faster perhaps, prettier certainly, but still designed around the convenience of the institution rather than the citizen. The ideal tax return need not be intellectually impressive. It should be almost boring. Login. Confirm identity. Verify pre-filled information. Answer a few relevant questions. Add anything missing. Review the tax computation. Reconcile assets with guided assistance. Press Submit. And finally receive a clear message: Your return has been successfully filed. Thank you. The purpose of a tax administration should not be to test how well citizens can navigate its internal architecture. Its task is to collect the correct tax while making voluntary compliance as painless as reasonably possible. Taxpayers willing to discharge their obligations should be assisted, not exhausted. After all, filing a return is already a legal duty. There is no reason to make it an obstacle course as well. ATHLETICS: PATHS TO GLORY. Pakistani triathletes Sana Arif (left) and Anisha Ali at the competition venue of the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan | Courtesy Sana Arif For Sana Arif, the journey to the Asian Games began with a sport she had only learnt a few years earlier. One of Pakistan’s pioneering women triathletes, Sana learnt to swim only in 2021, and went on to complete three Ironman 70.3 races — a gruelling endurance event combining a 1.9km swim, 90.1km of cycling and a 21.1km run. Born in Kuwait and raised in Lahore before returning to Kuwait, she had built her triathlon career largely through her own determination and training. In 2026, that journey took her to Japan, where she and fellow Pakistani triathlete Anisha Ali from Hunza became part of the country’s first women’s triathlon contingent at the Asian Games. They were joined by male teammates Ali Hassan, Mohid Sadiq Lone and Muhammad Mustaghis Noor. Sana’s teammate Anisha, 26, brought a very different sporting background to the team. A national-level athlete in judo, martial arts, rowing, boating, tug-of-war and fencing, she was no stranger to competition or rigorous training. But triathlon presented a new challenge, requiring her to master three disciplines simultaneously. Hailing from Gilgit-Baltistan, she says her upbringing around mountains taught her to embrace challenges rather than shy away from them. This was a mindset she carried with her to the Asian Games. For Pakistan’s first women triathletes at the Asian Games, the competition was about more than medals. It was about simply showing up… For Sana, the call that changed everything came almost by chance. She was in Pakistan on holiday when a friend told her that trials were being held for the Asian Games triathlon team. The timing was fortunate. She went along with a handful of other athletes, some stronger cyclists, others accomplished runners. But Sana had one advantage that mattered in a sport demanding proficiency in all three disciplines: she could swim well too. A week later, she received a call from the Pakistan Triathlon Federation. She had been selected to represent Pakistan at the Asian Games. The selection marked a first. Pakistan was sending women triathletes to compete at the continental Games, and Sana and Anisha would be part of a small pioneering team, entering a competition in which the country had never before had female representation. Following her selection, Sana trained largely on her own. The federation president remained in regular contact, checking on her progress and advising her on areas that needed attention. But, beyond that, there was no extensive national high-performance training programme in place. For a sport that combines swimming, cycling and running — each requiring its own technical skills, coaching and equipment — much of the responsibility remained with the athlete. Even meeting her teammates was a relatively new experience. Sana had crossed paths with two of them during the trials, but they had been too occupied with the selection process to get to know each other properly. Their team chemistry would develop only after they arrived in Japan. When they did, something unexpected happened. The team became a source of strength for one another. “We all knew who we were competing against,” Sana says. “Everyone was friendly, shared their experiences and supported wherever it was needed.” There was also an awareness that they were entering the competition at a disadvantage. “Though we were the weaker team compared to others, none of us even for a second thought of giving up. We fought till the end.” That spirit extended beyond Pakistan’s team. Sana recalls meeting athletes from other countries, including competitors who were among the best in their respective nations and had professional-level experience. Rather than making her feel inadequate, they did the opposite. When she explained that the sprint format was very different from the long-distance races she was accustomed to, they reassured her. “They were there to calm me down and tell me that it was all okay,” she says. Some even pointed out what Sana herself had begun to realise: simply being there had significance. She was representing a country that had never before sent women triathletes to the Asian Games. That, in itself, was an achievement. The experience in Japan also challenged some of the complaints circulating about conditions for athletes at the Games. For the triathletes, the arrangements were, Sana says, excellent. The team was based in Gamagori, a city designated specifically for the triathlon. Their accommodation was close to the race venue and the beach, with an island visible from their location and a running track in the surrounding garden. Food was another pleasant surprise. There was a dedicated table for Muslim athletes, as well as vegan options — details Sana appreciated as an athlete travelling from Pakistan. “The staff and people were great, and there was a lot of security too,” she recalls. The competition itself, however, brought the inevitable nerves. “It was great, but there was also a lot of anxiety, stress and excitement — mixed emotions,” she says. There were no medals for Pakistan. But for Sana, the value of the experience cannot be measured by a podium finish. If anything, the race revealed the gap between Pakistan’s ambitions and the support required to turn those ambitions into sustained international competitiveness. Her diagnosis is blunt: Pakistan needs to treat the triathlon as a long-term high-performance sport rather than something athletes prepare for only when a major Games approaches. “If Pakistan wants competitive Asian Games athletes, they shouldn’t start receiving support six months before the event,” she says. The problems begin with the basics. Athletes need proper equipment, financial support and structured training. Sana points out that Pakistani competitors arrived on rented bicycles, while the tri-suits provided to them were also not suitable for the demands of the sport. They were not even made from the appropriate fabric required for the triathlon. It is difficult, she argues, to expect international-level performances without first investing in the athletes expected to deliver them. Her point goes beyond the triathlon. Her teammate Anisha believes more Pakistani women are doing sports, but says many talented girls — particularly those from rural, remote and mountainous areas — still lack the facilities, coaching, financial support and safe spaces they need. Representation matters too, she says: seeing Pakistani women compete internationally can help young girls believe that sport is a possibility for them as well. Pakistan has repeatedly produced athletes who reach international competitions through individual determination, personal sacrifice and, often, their own financial resources. But competing at the highest level requires more than determination. It requires a system. For Sana, the Asian Games were therefore both an accomplishment and a starting point. The experience showed her what elite triathlon looks like and, perhaps more importantly, what Pakistan needs to build if it wants to compete seriously in the future. The response at home has largely been encouraging. There has been criticism too, as there inevitably is whenever Pakistani athletes compete without winning medals. Sana, however, has little interest in allowing that noise to define the experience. “People will always have something to say whether you win or lose,” she says. “No one understands your struggle, and that is okay.” What she does remember is the overwhelming support. “The amount of positivity I have received from everywhere is unexplainable.” For a first appearance, perhaps that is the more important result. Sana, Anisha and their teammates did not return from Japan with medals. They returned with something less tangible but potentially more consequential: proof that Pakistani women can enter a demanding sport like triathlon, compete on an international stage and hold their own against athletes from countries with far more developed systems. The next step is no longer simply getting them to the starting line. It is giving the next generation the training, equipment, coaching and financial support to arrive there ready to compete. The first women have now gone. The question is whether Pakistan will build a path for those who come next. The writer is a journalist, documentary filmmaker and radio correspondent.
