Profit rates on National Savings schemes increased from Oct 21. ISLAMABAD: The government has increased profit rates on several national savings schemes, including those for pensioners, senior citizens and families of martyrs, with the revised rates taking effect from October 21. According to the revised schedule issued by the Central Directorate of National Savings (CDNS), the profit rate on Behbood Savings Certificates, Pensioners’ Benefit Accounts and Shuhada’s Family Welfare Accounts has been raised to 12.96 per cent from 12.72pc. The increase will raise the monthly profit on an investment of Rs100,000 under these schemes to Rs1,080 from Rs1,060. Similarly, the profit rate on Regular Income Certificates has been increased to 12.12pc from 11.76pc. The revised rate will provide a monthly return of Rs1,010 on an investment of Rs100,000, compared with Rs980 previously. The profit rate on Special Savings Certificates has been increased to 12pc from 11.6pc for the first five profit payments. Under the revised schedule, investors will receive Rs6,000 on an investment of Rs100,000 every six months, while the sixth and final profit payment will be Rs6,400 at a rate of 12.8pc. The government has also raised cumulative profit rates on Defence Savings Certificates across different maturity periods. For six-year certificates, the cumulative return has increased to 88pc from 86pc, while the seven-year return has risen to 113pc from 109pc. Similarly, the eight-year return has increased to 142pc from 136pc, while the nine-year return has been raised to 176pc from 168pc. The cumulative return on certificates held for 10 years has increased to 215pc from 205pc. Profit rates on Short Term Savings Certificates have also been revised upwards. The rate on three-month certificates has increased to 11.12pc from 10.80pc, while the revised schedule provides rates of up to 11.72pc for longer maturities. The government has also increased returns on Sharia-compliant savings schemes. Profit rates on Sarwa Islamic Term Accounts now range between 11.84pc and 12.12pc for different maturities, while the rate on Sarwa Islamic Savings Accounts has been raised to 11.84pc from 11.33pc. However, the profit rate on ordinary Savings Accounts has been maintained at 10pc per annum. According to the official schedule, profits on national savings schemes are subject to withholding tax at 15pc for filers and 30pc for non-filers, while Zakat deductions apply where prescribed under the relevant rules.

ECP orders fresh schedule for Islamabad local government polls. ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday directed its office to prepare and issue the election programme for local government elections in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT). A five-member bench, headed by Chief Election Commissioner Sikandar Sultan Raja, issued the order while hearing a case concerning delays in holding local government elections in ICT. Members Nisar Ahmed Durrani, Shah Muhammad Jatoi, Babar Hassan Bharwana and Justice (retd) Ikramullah Khan were also part of the bench. The proceedings were initiated following a notice issued by the commission to the secretary of the Ministry of Interior and the chief commissioner of ICT. Secretary Interior Ahmed Raza Sarwar and Additional Deputy Commissioner Uzair Ali Khan, representing the chief commissioner of ICT, appeared before the commission, while the ECP was represented by its secretary, special secretary (policy), special secretary (law), ADG (LGE), ADG (law) and director (law). In its short order the Commission observed: “Accordingly, in exercise of its constitutional powers and functions under Articles 140A, 218(3), 219 and 220 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, read with Section 219 of the Elections Act, 2017, and under Sections 17 and 24 of the Islamabad Capital Territory Local Government Act, 2015, the Commission hereby directs the office to forthwith prepare and issue the Election Programme for the conduct of local government elections in the Islamabad Capital Territory, in accordance with the Islamabad Capital Territory Local Government Act, 2015, as legally in force, the Elections Act, 2017, and the rules made thereunder.” The ECP further directed the concerned office to ensure that all consequential steps were taken expeditiously and strictly in accordance with the law to facilitate the timely completion of the electoral process. Islamabad has been without an elected local government for more than five years . The only local government elections in the capital were held in 2015, with polls conducted for 50 union councils. The PML-N won the elections, and Sheikh Anser Aziz was elected the first mayor. The local government’s term expired in February 2021. Under Article 140-A of the Constitution and Section 219(4) of the Elections Act, 2017, the ECP is required to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of a local government’s term. However, fresh polls have been delayed amid repeated changes to the legal framework. The ECP conducted delimitations multiple times and issued election schedules on several occasions, only for them to be cancelled later — in one instance, a day before polling. Initially planned for 50 union councils (UCs), the number was increased to 101 and then to 125. In December 2022, elections were scheduled for Dec 31 that year on the basis of 101 UCs. However, just days before polling, the government amended the law to increase the number of UCs to 125, forcing the ECP to postpone the polls, citing logistical difficulties, despite an Islamabad High Court order to proceed. After a prolonged delay, the ECP announced a schedule for elections on Feb 15, 2026, for 125 UCs. However, in January 2026, President Asif Ali Zardari promulgated the Islamabad Capital Territory Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, which replaced the Metropolitan Corporation structure with three town corporations aligned with National Assembly constituencies, necessitating fresh delimitations. The ECP subsequently withdrew the schedule. The federal government pursued replacement legislation, with a parliamentary committee approving a bill in September. However, the legislation was not enacted before the ordinance lapsed. The ECP had earlier sent its feedback on the ICT Local Government Rules to the Interior Ministry on July 20, but the Law Ministry returned the draft, citing the expiry of the ordinance and the lack of authority to frame rules. The commission had sought the assistance of the interior secretary and the chief commissioner to determine how elections could proceed following the ordinance’s expiry. It has now decided to proceed under the 2015 Act, which remains in force. The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday ruled that Islamabad local government (LG) elections would be conducted under the ICT Local Government Act, 2015, adding that it would issue a schedule for the polls later in the day. A five-member commission, headed by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Sikandar Sultan Raja, conducted a hearing over multiple delays in the polls fixture for the past five years. Interior secretary and ECP officials appeared in the hearing as well. ECP Special Secretary Zafar Iqbal Malik said that delimitation of constituencies had been carried out six times and election schedules had been issued four times. The latest schedule, he added, was set for Oct 9, while the polling was originally planned for February this year. The Islamabad Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 lapsed on Sep 6, under which data and maps had been obtained and delimitation of constituencies was underway, Malik said. He added that final delimitations were published on Oct 14. Malik said that two reminder letters were sent to the interior ministry, informing it of the lapse of the ordinance. However, the rules for Islamabad LG polls had not been provided yet. “The Ministry of Law refused to vet the rules,” he claimed. Noting that the federal government has not enacted a local government law, he said that elections should be held according to the 2015 Act. He requested the ECP to authorise elections accordingly. ECP had sent its feedback on the Islamabad Local Government Rules to the Ministry of Interior on July 20, 2026, recommending that the legislation and rules be published accordingly. According to the ECP, the relevant legislation was approved by the standing committee on Sept 3, 2026. However, the ordinance expired on Sept 6, before the legislation could be enacted. Following Malik’s briefing, the interior secretary confirmed that the presented facts were accurate, but he argued, “If we revert to the 2015 law, everything will have to be scrapped”. CEC Raja responded, “If we revert to the 2015 law, the delimitations will not be affected”. Raja further told the hearing that the interior minister, interior secretary and the chief commissioner, on behalf of the ministerial committee, had provided an undertaking. “It appears that the government does not wish to hold local government elections in Islamabad,” he said. The CEC added, “The Constitution stipulates that elections must be held in accordance with the local government law. “Compelled by the circumstances, we are now issuing an order for the Islamabad local government elections.” The tenure of Islamabad’s local government expired in 2021, and the law required fresh elections to be held within 120 days. Recently, a high-level committee headed by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal and formed by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif recommended devolving powers from the federation to Islamabad as a federating unit. The committee proposed a provincial-style government for the capital. Under the proposal, the Islamabad Assembly, whenever formed, would have 27 members, including 21 directly elected representatives, with seven from each of the three National Assembly constituencies, five women on reserved seats and one minority member. All departments would function under the proposed assembly, except law and order and master planning, which would remain under the federal government. The assembly would elect a leader, to be called either the chief minister or mayor, who would serve as the chief executive. The chief commissioner would be replaced by a chief secretary.

US envoy to meet Putin after 'positive' talks with Zelensky. Washington’s envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg early Wednesday to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin following what US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as “ positive ” talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine. The trip by President Donald Trump’s special envoy is part of efforts to draw a line under a bitter feud between him and Zelensky over the war with Russia . After talks with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelensky thanked Washington on Tuesday for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes. The positive tone followed days of friction between Kyiv and Washington after Trump struck a diesel-supply deal with Putin and called for Zelensky to be replaced after Ukraine refused to stop hitting Russian oil refineries. “We are thankful that intelligence works,” Zelensky told reporters in Oslo, describing the early warnings as “very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians” when ballistic missiles were about to strike. Rubio said during a visit to India that Witkoff would next head to Russia after the “positive” talks with Zelensky. “He’ll now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to Saint Petersburg and share them with the Russian side — and let’s see if we can make some progress,” Rubio said. Witkoff’s planned meeting with Putin on Wednesday would include Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner participating virtually, a US official told AFP . Trump’s envoy was met at Pulkovo Airport in Saint Petersburg by the Kremlin’s adviser for international economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, according to news agencies. ‘Make a deal’ Trump said Tuesday that he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years earlier in Ukraine, though it was not clear if the request would be raised in Wednesday’s talks. “I’ve been talking to him at length. I’ve asked him to release him. Let’s see what happens,” Trump told journalists in Washington. Trump has also been keeping up the pressure on Ukraine, saying at the White House that he wanted Zelensky to “make a deal” with Russia, which is ramping up its strikes as a bitter winter looms. Trump, who called on Zelensky to resign last week, also criticised the Ukrainian president for not accepting terms he said he had offered during an infamous televised row in the Oval Office in February 2025. Ukraine reacted with dismay after Trump also waived sanctions against Russia’s war machine . The feud spiralled as Zelensky accused Trump of weakness, and then alleged that the United States was deliberately withholding vital intelligence and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles. Ukraine has also reported a reduction in speeds on Starshield, the US military satellite system it uses for battlefield communications and strikes on Russian-occupied territory. Trump has denied ordering a reduction in speeds on Starshield after Elon Musk — whose company SpaceX developed it — said the order could only have come from the White House. Rubio said Wednesday that Washington had no prior knowledge of the slowdown of the SpaceX satellite communications. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said in Mumbai. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that it was indeed Musk who ordered the slowdown in the military-grade version of Starlink. ‘Our future’ Witkoff’s meetings follow furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the row. Zelensky told US senators on Monday that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries, while the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature. Several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval, he said. Trump, whose Republican Party faces tough midterm elections as fuel prices soar, has accused Zelensky of a lack of effort to resolve the conflict. He said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war — sparking fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined. Zelensky insisted Tuesday that Kyiv needed to be represented at any meeting regarding Ukraine’s future. “If there are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations,” he said.

10 killed, 44 injured as passenger bus overturns on highway in Punjab's Rajanpur. DERA GHAZI KHAN: Ten people were killed and 44 others injured when a passenger bus overturned after hitting a road divider on the Indus Highway in Rajanpur district’s Rojhan tehsil, Rescue 1122 said. The accident occurred in the Bangla Hidayat area at around 5:45am. The bus was reportedly speeding when it collided with the divider and toppled over. The deceased include seven men, two women and a girl, Rescue 1122 said in an incident report. Of the 44 wounded, 38 were being treated at the Rajanpur District Headquarters (DHQ) Hospital, while four critically injured persons were referred to Dera Ghazi Khan and two seriously hurt to Rahim Yar Khan’s Sheikh Zayed Hospital. Rescue 1122 said it “responded promptly” upon receiving the emergency call and mobilised 10 ambulances and two rescue vehicles from Rajanpur, Jampur and Rojhan. It said 35 rescuers took part in the emergency response. Rajanpur Deputy Commissioner (DC) Imran Ranjha, the district police officer and the assistant commissioner also reached the site to oversee the situation and coordinate the response. DC Ranjha told Dawn that a case would be registered against the bus driver, who fled the scene after the incident, as well as its owner. On Monday, a road accident on Multan’s Bosan Road claimed the lives of five men in their 20s early after their speeding Toyota Corolla hit a road divider before crashing into the wall of a nearby plot and catching fire. According to Rescue 1122 , around 1,352 road traffic incidents, resulting in an average of 14 deaths, are reported per day across Punjab.

PM Shehbaz vows to strengthen Maldives ties for 'all time to come'; 20 MoUs signed. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday vowed to strengthen bilateral relations with the Maldives, as the two countries signed 20 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) during the visit of President Dr Mohamed Muizzu. Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit at the invitation of PM Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established in 1966. Addressing a joint press stakeout following the signing of 20 wide-ranging MoUs, PM Shehbaz said, “There is no doubt that the two countries [will] keep on strengthening these relations for all time to come.” The premier extended a “very warm welcome” to the visiting dignitary and his delegation. PM Shehbaz expressed his “warmest greetings and heartfelt affection to the people of Dhivehi Raajje, the land of islands, a nation whose spirit is as vast as the ocean that surrounds it,” hailing 60 years of diplomatic ties between the two countries. The prime minister noted that he and Muizzu, in their bilateral and delegation-level talks, discussed “all important issues which have direct bearing between our two brotherly countries and of course, regional and international issues”. “I am very happy to announce that we had a wonderful session, very productive and very fruitful discussions,” he remarked. PM Shehbaz noted that the conversations encompassed “economic and trade relations, our strategic defence cooperation, our support for training of our brothers and sisters from Maldives in Pakistan in various walks of life; police, defence, education, health and many other” fields. The prime minister went on to announce that both sides had agreed to raise their bilateral trade from $13.9 million — “just a fraction of our potential” — to $200m in the next two years. While highlighting that the two South Asian countries had “very strong” relations, coupled with a “long list of mutual achievements”, PM Shehbaz said both sides noted that their ties “do not reflect the true strength of our economic cooperation”. Thanking Muizzu for his “personal support in this behalf”, the premier went on to announce that Islamabad would support Malé in promoting the plantation of 5m trees in the Maldives by providing 100,000 olive cuttings and 100,000 seeds of various plant species within a mutually decided timeframe. Referring to the MoUs signed, he affirmed that he “will be very happy to personally work with [Muizzu] to translate these written MoUs into action with prompt decision-making and speedy implementation”. The prime minister declared that Pakistan was “absolutely ready to provide technical expertise to various segments of our mutual cooperation and, above all, Pakistan is very happy to learn that Maldives is moving forward speedily to establish data centres in other places”. “This is great news, and as a matter of good luck, Pakistan has also attained a reasonable level of expertise and professional capability in this field,” he added, noting that the country had set up data centres in various locations. He offered Pakistan’s “experience and our professional capabilities in this behalf” to the Maldives. PM Shehbaz noted that a large number of Maldivian students were receiving education in Pakistani universities and colleges, particularly in the field of healthcare, and that 250 Pakistani doctors and other paramedics were serving in the Maldives. “This shall continue in future with bigger numbers so that whatever requirements you have, we as a brotherly country would be more than happy to fulfil those requirements willingly and with utmost sincerity of purpose,” the prime minister assured Muizzu. Speaking on international developments, PM Shehbaz commended the Maldives’ “unwavering” support for the Palestinian cause, adding that Islamabad remains fully committed to the Palestinians’ right of self-determination and the establishment of an independent state of Palestine. The premier further said he briefed Muizzu on Pakistan’s principled position on occupied Jammu and Kashmir, declaring Islamabad’s support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. “Till they have won their struggle and gotten the right of self-determination, Pakistan shall continue to support them diplomatically and, of course, support them at all international forums till they become an independent sovereign country as per UNSC resolutions, and their sacrifice will not go to waste at all,” he said. The prime minister also expressed Pakistan’s “serious concern” over India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance in April 2025, pointing out that it was a violation of an international binding treaty. “Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponised or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he stated. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan has made it “abundantly clear at various forums ”, including the UN General Assembly last month, that water was a “red line” for the country. “Waterflows in any canal or ocean, sea or straits, carries trade, commerce, message of prosperity and progress, and not threats, confrontations and conflicts,” he said. “Water is a lifeline for humanity […] so this should be known to all and sundry that any violation in this behalf will be regarded by Pakistan as an act of war,” the prime minister warned. Concluding his remarks, PM Shehbaz said Muizzu’s visit had given Pakistan-Maldives relations “new purpose and new momentum”. He remarked, “The same ocean that touches the shores of Karachi and Gwadar embraces the islands of the Maldives. “For centuries, its waves have carried traders, scholars and travellers between our lands. Today, they carry the renewed promise of our wonderful friendship whose finest chapters are yet to be written.” In his comments, Muizzu appreciated PM Shehbaz, the government and people of Pakistan for “their exceptional warmth and gracious hospitality”. He added that his visit coming on the 60-year mark of Pakistan-Maldives diplomatic relations made it “particularly significant”. The 60 years have been marked by warmth, friendship and shared perspectives, he said. “This visit takes place after a decade-long interval. It offers us an important opportunity not simply to celebrate the friendship of the past but to define the partnership of the future,” Muizzu said. Stressing on the close relations between the two countries, he said, “Only two such longstanding friends could have talked so widely and agreed on so much about our future together”. Muizzu said, for him, the talks represented a “clear shared ambition to move the Maldives-Pakistan partnership into a new era”. He said the discussions encompassed several sectors including trade and investment; health and education; environment, fisheries and agriculture; youth and sports; policing and defence; training and capacity-building; and tourism. He said he was pleased about the signing of 20 MOUs. “These memoranda will open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results. “Our next step, of course, is to translate these understandings into tangible opportunities and meaningful benefits for the people of both nations.” Muizzu said he endorsed the goal to take the two countries’ bilateral trade quantum from $13m to $200m in two years. “The Maldives and Pakistan are worlds of untapped potential for each other,” the Maldivian president said. He reaffirmed that the two countries would take a “firm step in the right direction”, adding that Thursday’s business forum would provide an opportunity to bring together business leaders, inventors and innovators from both countries to turn the friendship into mutually beneficial investments. He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well. He further said that the two countries’ leaders saw “considerable potential in halal and Muslim-friendly tourism”. Muizzu appreciated Pakistan’s scholarships and placements for Maldivian students, adding that the leaders would broaden the opportunities further, especially in artificial intelligence, digitisation and future technologies as well as health. “We want our next generation to be prepared for the future and be prepared to shape that future.” Muizzu stressed that climate change was “not an abstract environmental concern” for the Maldives. Instead, he said, “it is a direct challenge to our security, our development and our future”. He welcomed cooperation with Pakistan in areas of climate resilience, conservation, sustainable waste management and renewable energy. He thanked PM Shehbaz for his announcement of donations to help the Maldives plant 5m trees in five years. “Our nations share a commitment to advancing common interests through constructive engagements.” He said the Maldives remained committed to revitalising the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, adding that “rebuilding trust, encouraging meaningful dialogue and strengthening mutual understanding are essential to unlocking the full potential of regional cooperation”. He further expressed the Maldives’ “unequivocal and steadfast solidarity” with Palestinians and their “legitimate right to self-determination”. Muizzu also commended Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts “to promote dialogue, de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and a just and lasting peace” in the Middle East. Concluding his remarks, he said, “For 60 years, Pakistan has stood as a trusted friend of the Maldives.” The two countries have now agreed to “build a new era of partnership on the foundations of our six decades of friendship”, he said. The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University Islamabad. PM Shehbaz had noted that the degree recognised Muizzu’s “sagacious and wise leadership and your great public service to your people in the Maldives”. 20 MoUs signed Pakistan and the Maldives on Wednesday signed a series of MoUs aimed at deepening bilateral relations in multiple sectors, including defence, IT, cybersecurity, health, education, social protection, agriculture and tourism, among others. PM Shehbaz and Muizzu witnessed the ceremony as the representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents. The two countries signed an MoU on cooperation in the fields of information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital skills, and technology and innovation. An MoU was inked to strengthen cooperation in combating illicit trafficking and abuse of narcotic drugs. The two sides also signed an MoU on social protection as well as on health cooperation and between Maldives Food and Drug Authority and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan. Both nations signed MoUs focused on the recruitment of health professionals, strengthening defence ties and maritime security cooperation. With a view to boosting agricultural cooperation, an MoU was signed on the subject between the two countries, besides another one on promoting fisheries cooperation. To promote ties in technical and vocational education, an MoU on collaboration to promote technical and vocational education and training was signed, while another MoU was inked to promote educational cooperation. The representatives of Pakistan and the Maldives also exchanged documents on MoUs on cooperation in the field of youth and sports development, air connectivity, tourism and in the field of arts, culture and heritage. The MoUs were signed between the National College of Policy and Law Enforcement of the Maldives Police Service and National Police Academy, Islamabad; Civil Service Commission of Maldives and the Federal Public Service Commission of Pakistan; and Civil Service Commission of Maldives and Civil Service Academy (CSA) of Pakistan. In order to boost commercial engagement, an MoU was signed between the Maldives State Trading Organisation (STO) and Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) for cooperation in trade of agriculture commodities, food and other products, besides signing another pact aimed at boosting cooperation in the field of environment. Prior to the MoU signing ceremony, Muizzi was welcomed at Prime Minister House with a guard of honour. He held introductions with federal ministers, while PM Shehbaz also greeted the Maldivian delegation. According to a statement by PM Office (PMO), the prime minister extended a “warm welcome to the esteemed guest”, followed by a guard of honour by smartly turned-out contingents of all three armed forces. The visiting dignitary also planted a sapling at PM House, and prayers were offered for the progress and prosperity of both countries. An earlier statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO) said Muizzu will meet President Asif Ali Zardari and will also hold “restricted and delegation-level” talks with PM Shehbaz. A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment. Meeting with Dar Earlier in the day, Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called on Muizzu, welcoming him and his delegation to Pakistan, FO said on X. Dar “underscored the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade, investment, education, climate change and tourism”, FO said. DPM Dar also welcomed the Maldivian business delegation in the Maldives-Pakistan Business Forum and “expressed hope that B2B engagements would yield concrete trade and investment opportunities”. Muizzu, speaking to Dar, “expressed Maldives’ desire to deepen its close relations with Pakistan and explore new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation”, FO said. Last month, the Maldives’ parliamentary speaker Abdul Raheem Abdullah met with Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Rawalpindi. In 2015 , former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-PM Nawaz Sharif.

Nigeria confirms its first Ebola case is Bundibugyo strain. The first Ebola case detected in Nigeria is the Bundibugyo strain, which is behind a major DR Congo outbreak , and the patient is a diplomat, an emergency meeting heard on Wednesday. The case in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda to the capital Abuja on Oct 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said. Since the Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever has spread to several countries across the continent, including to neighbouring Uganda. “We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo,” Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC said. The World Health Organisation (WHO) also confirmed that it was the Bundibugyo strain , for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment. “This person is actually a diplomat,” another official said, adding the patient has deteriorated into “multi-organ failure”. The director general of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, warned on Tuesday of “an extremely serious threat” as Kenya also declared its ninth Ebola case. In several months, the DRC’s Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country’s history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases, according to the health authorities. Nigeria has identified 44 contacts that are being monitored, while intensifying efforts to find other people who may have been exposed. The WHO said in a statement that infection prevention and control was being “ramped up” at the private hospital where the patient sought care.

Macron takes aim at Trump for using France riots for election gain. President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday took an apparent swipe at counterpart Donald Trump of exploiting France’s riots for advantage in the US midterm election battle, as Paris prepared for more protests this weekend. Macron, speaking during a visit to Qatar, implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also in election mode , made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain, though he did not name either leader. “There are people who campaign at France’s expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha. Macron made his remarks as he and his government struggled to get on top of a crisis that has scarred France’s image both abroad and in financial markets, six months ahead of presidential elections to choose his successor. France’s government has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings. Trump has sought to link the “revolution” in France to “migrants, jihadists, and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging. He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies, as a conservative voice, with surveys putting her as the frontrunner in France’s presidential race. Trump’s ally Netanyahu, facing his own tough election battle, on Tuesday argued that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France’s protests. Curfews The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held on Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France. Since the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of further cost-of-living demonstrations this coming Saturday, Macron’s government has warned it will brook no further violence. Authorities in Paris and several other cities imposed nighttime curfews Monday and Tuesday in certain zones prone to protests or looting. Macron said that on Thursday he would chair a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials to receive a “detailed account” of what happened last weekend. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organising marches, has vowed a “massive” police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation. The convulsion in France, the EU’s second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country’s growing debt pile and deficit. The yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bond has been rising, and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell. On Friday, the Moody’s ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France’s public debt. The country’s political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year. Le Pen leads race The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff. France’s neighbours Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there. Macron said that “we don’t need a state of emergency” that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that “we have the means” already at authorities’ disposal, such as curfews. While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11pm (2am PKT). “It’s quite disconcerting,” said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But “if it can prevent further acts of vandalism… then yes, I think it’s a good thing”, he said. The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend’s demonstrations announced on Wednesday that it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille square. The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on Nov 5. The images broadcast around the world of France’s street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

Man accused of running over Multan teenager killed in alleged CCD encounter. The suspect accused of running over and fatally injuring a 14-year-old boy in Multan was killed in an alleged encounter with the Crime Control Department (CCD) in Bahawalpur early on Wednesday, police said. The suspect, identified as Tauqeer, had allegedly escaped from police custody while on remand, a CCD spokesperson said. A Multan court on Tuesday granted police three-day physical remand of the suspect. The suspect was accused of hitting the victim, who used to work for him, with his car in a private housing society. He was arrested on Monday and presented before Judicial Magistrate Saadia Aslam on Tuesday. According to the spokesperson, the CCD personnel attempted to stop two individuals riding a motorcycle on Bahawalpur’s Northern Bypass when an exchange of fire ensued, leaving the suspect dead. On Tuesday, police requested a 14-day physical remand of the suspect for investigation. However, the judicial magistrate granted the police a three-day remand. At the time, Multan City Police Officer (CPO) Akhtar Farooq said while speaking to the media that raids were being conducted for the arrest of a second suspect. “We all are in deep pain,” the CPO said, adding that the orphan boy had been “subjected to barbarity”. The CCTV footage of the incident shows a boy running on the road after spotting a car. The car is seen swerving and chasing the boy, eventually hitting him. The boy, who fell, then rams into the gate of a nearby house and dies on impact. A case was registered on the state’s behalf at Multan’s DHA police station. The first information report (FIR) named two suspects and invoked Sections 302 (intentional murder) and 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. According to the FIR, the teenage boy had been working for the suspects and was being trained as an electrician. His cousin told police that the boy had reportedly faced violence and threats by the suspects, the FIR said, adding that the 14-year-old was fleeing when the suspects pursued him in a car and hit him. Police arrested one of the suspects while the other escaped, the FIR stated. It added that their vehicle had been taken into custody.

‘Where are the courts?’: Killing of Multan suspect in alleged CCD encounter sparks concern among lawyers, journalists. The death of a suspect, allegedly during an exchange of fire with Punjab’s Crime Control Department (CCD), sparked questions from lawyers and journalists on Wednesday regarding extrajudicial killings and due process. The CCD, established last year, has been criticised by human rights advocates and civil society members for a high number of casualties. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) alleged earlier this year that the CCD has adopted a “deliberate policy of staged police encounters leading to extrajudicial killings”. In response, the department termed the claims as unfounded and contrary to the department’s operational framework. The suspect who was killed in the latest alleged encounter was accused of running over a 14-year-old boy, who worked for him, with his car in a private housing society in Multan. That incident also sparked anger among the public, with a police officer saying the teenager had been “subjected to barbarity”. The CCD claimed that the suspect, identified as Tauqeer, had escaped from its custody after it was granted the man’s three-day physical remand . According to the department, he was found dead after an exchange of fire when its personnel attempted to stop two individuals riding a motorcycle on Bahawalpur’s Northern Bypass. The alleged encounter came on the heels of another incident in Islamabad where the police claimed a suspect was killed when his accomplices opened fire on a police team transporting him. Lawyers and journalists took to X to voice their concerns over the rule of law. Advocate Nida Usman Chaudhry, founder of Women in Law, said extrajudicial killings were not the kind of justice people expected from the state, describing them as another example of the state failing its citizens. “When we demand ‘justice’, what we mean is through the rules of fair investigation, fair trial and due process,” she said. Journalist and writer Shabbir Dar said extrajudicial killings “exposed the failure of the criminal justice system that consumes billions in public funds but has lost the confidence of both the public and those in power”. Former human rights minister Shireen Mazari also weighed in on the incident, asking in a post on X: “‘Out of control’ is the new control?” A post from PML-N MPA Hina Parvez Butt, which was later deleted, prompted criticism as well. “This is [Punjab Chief Minister] Maryam Nawaz sahiba ’s government; justice is served immediately here,” wrote Butt, sharing screengrabs of a TV report regarding the Bahawalpur encounter. A screengrab of a now-deleted post made on X by PML-N MPA Hina Parvez Butt on Oct 21, 2026. Journalist Hasnaat Malik criticised Butt’s post, questioning the need to spend enormous amounts of funds on courts if justice was to be delivered in this manner. “It would have been better if punishment was given after fulfilling all legal requirements,” he said. Advocate Abdul Moiz Jaferii took aim at Butt, who heads the Punjab Women Protection Authority, for “celebrating” the suspect’s killing. “This is not justice, it is vengeance. And an admission of guilt,” the lawyer said in a post on X. Journalist Absa Komal termed “celebrating extrajudicial killings” as “legal and moral bankruptcy”. “When the police themselves become judge and executioner, it is not the rule of law, but the law of the jungle,” the former DawnNews anchor said, sharing a post about both recent incidents. Senior journalist Naimat Khan pointed out that a “lawmaker from the ruling party is celebrating an extrajudicial killing of an accused person who should have been tried in a court of law to deliver justice to the victim”. “The extrajudicial killing of even a guilty person reflects a profound mistrust in the justice system and government and undermines the rule of law,” he stressed. Journalist Maryam Nawaz Khan termed it a “total failure of the system”. “When the state relies solely on CCD or police encounters, it’s an admission that our judicial system is dead,” she contended while commenting on Butt’s post. TV anchor Nadia Mirza also questioned the characterisation of the killing as justice. “Oh!! so now you are calling an extrajudicial killing JUSTICE. Strange … where are courts?” she said in a post on X. Journalist Javeria Siddique highlighted that extrajudicial killings directly violated the rule of law, adding that a civilised society punished people through courts rather than “encounters, enforced disappearances or targeted eliminations”. Shazia Nimai, chairperson of the Sindh Women Lawyers Alliance, called for the suspect to have been tried in court, saying Punjab police should have produced him before a judge to face trial and sentencing. “How is it possible that handcuffed suspects, surrounded by armed policemen, manage to escape in case after case?” she asked.

Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin mloukili Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Commentary / Europe 15 October 2026 12 minutes Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin Criminal groups have taken over swathes of the Amazon, fuelling violence and environmental destruction through illicit business. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group shows how the EU and member states can curb these activities and ecological damage. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Download PDF Full Report Download Full Report Select your download language English Spanish Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Amazon The Amazon, the world’s largest tropical rainforest, is vital for planetary wellbeing. But it is also the source of several commodities, often obtained and sold illegally, that are in high commercial demand. Expanding markets for gold, wood, beef, critical minerals, wildlife, soy and cocaine, among other licit and illicit goods, have resulted in widespread environmental harm, including deforestation and contamination of soil and waterways . The alarming result is that parts of the Amazon are now releasing more carbon into the atmosphere than they absorb, contributing to global warming. Meanwhile, the crime rings involved in supplying some of these items have tightened their grip on swathes of the Amazon , particularly its rivers and estuaries. The profits they reap allow them to challenge state authority and co-opt officials. They use lethal violence against Indigenous and other residents to consolidate their hold. Europe is a major destination for many of the Amazon’s illicit or illegally produced goods. It is also at the forefront of efforts to contain global climate change, a cause that depends for its success on preserving ecosystems such as the Amazon. Yet European governments have been hesitant to address the intersection of trafficking and organised crime in the Amazon, which makes the job of preserving the rainforest much harder. The EU and its member states should work closely with South American partners to improve security cooperation, harmonise legal norms around environmental crimes, back Indigenous community responses aimed at curtailing illicit businesses and support the creation of legal livelihoods in the Amazon. This set of initiatives could help weaken the criminal groups bringing violence to the Amazon and limit the environmental damage they cause. Aerial view taken during a Greenpeace flyover of illegal mining areas in Kayapo indigenous territory in Para state, Brazil, on 19 March, 2025. AFP / Pablo Porciuncula Organised Crime in the Jungle Over the last decade, criminal groups have extended their reach across the Amazon, both to exploit its natural riches and to use its rivers to carry goods to seaports for shipment to European and Asian buyers. Governments in the Amazon basin have taken action to stop these activities, seeking to curb both the environmental degradation they cause and the attendant violence, but shifting political priorities and lack of resources have meant that the effects of their campaigns have been uneven. Criminals take advantage of discrepancies among the various countries’ penal codes to avoid running afoul of regulations and facing prosecution. For instance, Brazil prohibits the commercial export of many wildlife species, while Guyana and Suriname permit it under a quota. As a result, traffickers can catch animals in Brazil, move them across one of the borders and ship them legally from Guyana and Suriname without needing to forge documents. Shifting Drug Routes Drug traffickers have long taken advantage of the Amazon’s vast expanses and weak state presence to cultivate and process coca crops and transport cocaine, which they then send across the Atlantic Ocean. Despite prohibition measures, South American production of the narcotic is at an all-time high, spurred by a boom in consumption in Europe. In response, Europe has continued to focus its law enforcement efforts on drug interdictions , largely as shipments approach the continent’s ports. The U.S., for its part, has turned to military firepower, launching a wave of attacks on alleged drug-carrying boats along routes across the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, killing almost 240 suspected traffickers so far. Some reports claim that these U.S. strikes have pushed additional quantities of drugs onto Amazon routes, but more research is needed to verify such a shift. That said, evidence does show that drug markets in the rainforest are more robust than ever: in Brazil alone, there was a 574 per cent increase in cocaine seizures in the country’s nine Amazon basin states between 2019 and 2024. With the state’s reach limited in much of the Amazon, traffickers move cocaine from Bolivia, Colombia and Peru to ports in the Guianas and Brazil. Barcarena, where the Amazon empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Source: Crisis Group research; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP The limited reach of the state in much of the Amazon means that traffickers face few obstacles in transporting cocaine, which is produced mostly in Bolivia, Colombia and Peru, to ports in the Guianas (as the north-eastern part of South America comprising French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname is known) and Brazil, from where they ship it to Europe, either directly or via West Africa . Barcarena, the Brazilian town where the Amazon river system empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Cocaine leaves through the Vila do Conde container terminal concealed in legitimate cargo, usually without the exporter’s knowledge. Recent shipments have been found in açaí , quartz and soy meal consignments bound for Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Australia. Crisis Group has previously written about how criminal groups in the region collaborate, with each playing a role in transforming coca into cocaine, moving it through the Amazon and distributing it worldwide. These networks encompass Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho in Brazil; the National Liberation Army or ELN, Comandos de la Frontera and other FARC dissident groups in Colombia; and Los Lobos and Los Choneros in Ecuador. All these organisations have employed violence and payoffs to quash local resistance and rid themselves of state agents who get in the way of doing business. But, reflecting what is happening elsewhere in Latin America, competition among criminal groups in the Amazon is also becoming lethal. Along the Orinoco River and Río Negro, shared by Colombia and Venezuela, a long-time alliance between the ELN and FARC dissidents of the Segunda Marquetalia came to an end in August 2025 , triggering clashes in which the groups used landmines and drones. As rivals jostle for control of markets, violence is likely to get worse. The expansion of organised crime is particularly pernicious for young residents of areas where they operate. These groups often hire children and adolescents to help with logistical tasks, paying them in drugs rather than cash. The kids then sell the drugs, causing substance abuse to rise in riverine villages. Along the Amazon River in Colombia, for example, Indigenous Ticuna people report that drug sale points have cropped up in rural areas. With no harm reduction programs in place, elders worry about the future of their children and the long-term effects on their communities. Gold and Other Commodities Many drug trafficking organisations have diversified into illegal gold mining, as rising prices for the metal have made it lucrative , with sales often raking in more income for criminals than cocaine. Illicit gold extraction can destroy ecosystems, as miners raze forests and pollute rivers and their banks with mercury (used to separate bits of gold from sediment). Mining sites have also been linked to grave human rights abuses, including violence against Indigenous leaders, sexual exploitation and child labour. Besides being highly profitable, gold is appealing because the product itself is easily transported and difficult to trace to its source. Even if illegally extracted, it can be funnelled into the legal supply chain at little risk just by forging paperwork. Criminal organisations seize this opportunity to “clean” drug trafficking proceeds by either investing in illegal gold mining or purchasing gold directly. The Guianas are a hub for these practices, as local regulations allow miners to absorb gold extracted in Venezuela and then re-export it as if it was locally produced. Over the past decade, much of Venezuela’s illicit gold has reached Switzerland and Belgium in this way , with large quantities also transiting Amsterdam. Security forces throughout the Amazon region are also concerned about Venezuela’s growing role in laundering illegal gold from Brazil and Colombia. After Caracas adopted a new mining law and U.S. sanctions authorities provided a licence for sales from the state company Minerven, illicit gold sellers have sought to mix their products into this newly legal pipeline for international sales. Law enforcement officials have told Crisis Group that “dirty gold” from other Amazon countries often passes through European airports for sale to refiners and minerals traders in countries including Germany and Italy. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. The ELN-Segunda Marquetalia fighting, which has spread from Venezuela into Colombia, was sparked by contests over gold and critical mineral mining sites as well as narcotics. In April, for example, these two groups battled in the Venezuelan municipality of Cedeño, displacing dozens of families . Other coveted minerals can also be found in the Amazon, including coltan, tin and tungsten. More than half the world’s critical mineral deposits are located on or in proximity to Indigenous lands. In Brazil, for instance, companies have sought permission to look for critical minerals in or near almost 44 per cent of the country’s Indigenous territories. The people residing in remote areas of the rainforest are often the victims of violence and other abuses committed by armed groups undertaking exploration. In Venezuela’s Amazonas and Bolívar states, coltan, tin and tungsten are mined in Indigenous lands that are under guerrilla control ; residents told Crisis Group that child labour, sexual violence and summary executions are frequent. To make matters worse, Venezuelan state forces in the area are reportedly collecting kickbacks from the groups, rather than protecting the vulnerable, and at times enriching themselves by taking more direct control of mines. Meanwhile, cattle ranching, land grabbing and industrial agriculture, the main drivers of Amazon deforestation, continue to grow as criminal groups launder money by investing in land, livestock and agribusiness. In Brazil, the expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching accounted for 99 per cent of native vegetation loss in 2025. What is at Stake for the EU Europe is tied to the violence and environmental damage done by resource extraction and trafficking in the Amazon because it is a major customer for the commodities in question. At the same time, the EU presents itself as a partner in forest protection and sustainable development as ways to mitigate the effects of climate change. But the attention paid by European leaders to the Amazon crisis has been fitful, due partly to sheer distance and partly to preoccupation with more immediate problems like the Ukraine and Middle East wars. European governments are also inclined to avoid engaging with Latin America in ways that might upset the U.S., particularly under the Trump administration, which has made clear it wants Washington to be the dominant influence in the Western Hemisphere. Even in law enforcement cooperation, which Washington seems to favour, Europe is keen to avoid any initiatives resembling U.S. backing for lethal armed force. The health of the rainforest and its inhabitants, however, is crucial for the EU in several ways. In recognition of its importance to achieving Europe’s climate goals, the EU-funded Amazonia+ program currently supports eight Amazon countries in tackling deforestation, forest degradation and wildfires. Germany and France, meanwhile, have pledged up to 1.5 billion euros combined to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new Brazilian-led fund that pays countries for each hectare of forest they preserve. Furthermore, in March the EU adopted a binding 2040 target of slashing net emissions by 90 per cent from 1990 levels. While at least 85 per cent of that cut must be achieved domestically, up to 5 per cent of the remainder may be met by buying carbon credits from projects outside the EU (each credit will represent one tonne of emissions cut, or carbon removed somewhere else on Europe’s behalf). Cooperating with states and civil society in the Amazon could help meet these objectives. Another issue of acute concern for Europe is critical minerals. The EU and its member states are keen to diversify imports of these minerals , which have important applications in the green, digital, defence and aerospace sectors, and the Amazon is well positioned to form part of its supply chains. At present, Europe relies heavily on China, which builds more than 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth magnets and dominates refining of these elements. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act aims to ensure EU access to a secure and sustainable supply of these materials. Of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical raw materials list , 25 are extracted in Latin America. Brussels has already established partnerships with two Latin American countries, Argentina and Chile , aimed at boosting cooperation on critical raw mineral extraction, while negotiations with Brazil are under way. Brazil already supplies over 80 per cent of the EU’s niobium, with most of its unprocessed copper coming from Brazil, Peru and Chile. Responsible mining investment in Latin America could help European countries acquire these valuable elements while limiting the harmful consequences for local communities and the environment. The EU has already adopted rules to address concerns about criminal profiteering and abuses in the mineral supply chain. But these are restricted in scope, and some have yet to kick in. The EU’s Conflict Minerals Regulation requires importers to carry out due diligence to guarantee their supply chains are not funding armed groups, violence or abuses, though it applies only to tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, not the full list of critical raw materials. Another initiative, the Critical Raw Materials Act , allows the EU to fast-track certain projects, so long as they put environmental, social and human rights safeguards in place. Yet only a small subset of projects is covered, and there is too little transparency about which ones are chosen and how to ensure compliance. Enforcement of the landmark Deforestation Regulation, meant to bar soy, cattle, timber and other commodities from the EU market unless proven to have no connection to deforestation, has now been pushed back twice under pressure from industry and trade partners. It is now set to enter force in December. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities. Arguably, however, European states’ main concern is the cocaine pouring into their cities from South America, including via the Amazon trafficking route. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities like Antwerp and Rotterdam, as well as in other hotspots in Italy, Spain, France and Germany. Crisis Group’s conversations with European officials suggest that curbing drug trafficking is a pressing policy concern for many governments and voters. Europe’s efforts to address drug trafficking in Latin America have already touched on the Amazon route, mostly through the now completed COPOLAD program. In Peru, for example, the program funded the creation of an early warning system to flag environmental crimes and criminal threats to human rights defenders. EU cooperation initiatives such as EL PAcCTO 2.0 have also funded projects to boost cross-border law enforcement cooperation on illegal gold mining. In late 2025, EL PAcCTO, Interpol and the Dutch police environmental crime unit aided Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname in the first transnational operation to this effect , known as the Guyana Shield, which resulted in 198 arrests and seizures of illicit goods. Germany, for its part, has long funded the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), while other European countries take part in specific initiatives on security in the region. France, for example, has deployed a liaison officer to the international police cooperation centre in Manaus, Brazil, created following the ACTO’s 2023 Belém Declaration . The EU is also supporting efforts to enhance border management and multinational frontier cooperation as well as to counter human trafficking in Latin America through EUROFRONT , including Amazon-region borders between Colombia and Ecuador. To tackle the challenges facing the Amazon, the EU and its member states should: Help improve law enforcement cooperation and legal harmonisation. The EU and its member states should pair seizures of illicit commodities with asset recovery and money laundering investigations that target the European counterparts of local criminal syndicates. The EU should also step up support for multinational law enforcement and expand port and container security cooperation with Amazon exit points such as Barcarena and the Guianas, where interdiction is weakest and cocaine shipments are on the rise. The EU and its partners should also push for legal harmonisation – eg, of illicit trafficking definitions in various penal codes – within the ACTO and Andean Community. To this end, the EU should support a proposal spearheaded by Brazil to add environmental crimes to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. Strengthen legislation governing gold and critical minerals markets. Critical raw materials refined outside the EU and imported as finished components fall outside the EU’s regulatory frameworks on conflict minerals and deforestation, while unrefined rare earths and bauxite are not covered at all. To ensure that its imports are not linked to criminal activity, the EU, its member states and its partners should support efforts such as those led by Brazil’s Federal Police and Colombia’s geological service to build gold and/or critical mineral traceability systems. The EU should also support law enforcement efforts targeting secondary products used in illicit mining, such as mercury, fuel, cyanide, explosives and mining equipment. Design a holistic approach toward the Amazon. The withdrawal of U.S. development aid has left gaps in environmental support and programming for alternative livelihoods in communities across the Amazon. While Europe cannot completely fill those spaces, the EU should focus support on market access, education and climate adaptation, particularly in coca-growing and gold-mining regions. Global Gateway – the EU’s strategy for financing infrastructure and connectivity projects in partner countries – should channel private investment toward sustainable infrastructure that could help make legal activities such as small-scale farming and fishing more commercially feasible, reducing the incentives for local communities to participate in illicit activity. Simultaneously, to slow deforestation, the EU should double down on results-based strategies such as that of the TFFF, which offers direct benefits to states that succeed in conserving forested areas. Back Indigenous governance. The EU and its member states should encourage capitals across the region to work closely with Indigenous organisations in monitoring illegal activities in remote jungles, since they are well placed to spot criminal activity where state security institutions are weak or absent.
